item.title: Eagles News: Commanders get bad news ahead of hosting Philadelphia
item.description: Philadelphia Eagles news and links for 10/31/26.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation!

With Daron Payne getting hurt and Javon Kinlaw already ruled out, the Commanders are set to be without their top two interior defensive linemen against the Eagles in Week 8. Philadelphia is banged up at running back … but Saquon Barkley is going to give it a go with only Elijah Mitchell and Jaydon Blue backing him up. Seems like the Eagles will have opportunities to run the ball against this Washington defense.

Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links …

Sources: Commanders’ Daron Payne likely IR-bound after practice injury – ESPN

Washington Commanders defensive tackle Daron Payne suffered a significant foot injury in practice Friday that likely will land him on injured reserve, sources told NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport and Mike Garafolo. The injury occurred during a team drill on a day that is considered a light practice. He’ll undergo more tests Saturday, but initial X-rays showed significant damage, a team source told ESPN. Depending on what the additional tests reveal, it’s possible Payne, who’s in the final year of his contract, will be done for the season. It’s yet another blow for the Commanders, who are 1-4-1 in a pivotal third season for coach Dan Quinn. They also will be without their other starting defensive end, Javon Kinlaw, for Sunday’s game against the Philadelphia Eagles (2-5) because of a knee injury.

Eagles at Commanders Game Preview: 5 questions and answers with the Week 8 enemy – BGN

The Philadelphia Eagles are riding a five-game losing streak entering Sunday Night Football against the Washington Commanders, a team they beat in the season opener. Can the Birds win a game for the first time since September 20? In order to preview this Week 8 NFC East battle, I reached out to our enemies over at Hogs Haven. The amicable Andrew Y kindly kindly took the time to answer my questions about this upcoming battle. Let’s take a look at the answers.

NFC East Mixtape VOL. 202: Can Dallas build? | PHI/WAS | Giants Outlook – NFC East Mixtape

It feels like the NFC East has been whittled down to two teams, and only one of them is playing this week in the Dallas Cowboys. Is there any way that they can build on Monday night by beating the (for them) big, bad Arizona Cardinals? Meanwhile… the Philadelphia Eagles and Washington Commanders are about to play one of the least exciting Sunday Night Football games we have ever seen. Who wants it more? Who wants it least? And while the New York Giants are off this week times are very exciting for them. Big Blue View’s Ed Valentine joins RJ Ochoa and Brandon Lee Gowton for an update on how things are going with the G-Men. You can see that we have a BRAND NEW NFC East Mixtape YouTube Channel so make sure to subscribe as the show will live here exclusively in video format. AND you can also listen to the show! On Blogging The Boys and/or Bleeding Green Nation podcast feeds as well as the SB Nation NFL Show feed!

Washington Commanders vs Philadelphia Eagles Week 8: Five Questions with Bleeding Green Nation – Hogs Haven

On defense, the Eagles are healthier, primarily dealing with injury to LB Jihaad Campbell, who has been ruled out of week 8. Despite their health, the Eagles defense has declined precipitously in 2026 to be the 5th-worst pass defense by yards allowed and the 6th-worst rush defense by yards allowed, as well as ranking poorly in advanced stats. One theory behind the defense’s decline is that they are getting beat up from being on the field all the time due to the collapse of the offense. Through Week 7, the Eagles defense has been on the field for 67.3 plays/game, 4th-most in the NFL. Certain players have had a harder time than others, with slot CB Cooper DeJean suffering from a high missed-tackle rate and notable drop in coverage quality. I asked Brandon Lee Gowton of Bleeding Green Nation five questions to better understand the state of the Eagles and what to look for in this game.

Why the NFL didn’t flex the Eagles vs. Commanders out of ‘Sunday Night Football’ – SB Nation

For 20 years, the NFL has made Sunday Night Football on NBC the marquee prime-time game of the weekend. Flexible scheduling was one of the selling points of SNF on NBC, with the league having the ability to swap out lackluster games for higher quality matchups. For several years, SNF has had its flex scheduling window opened in Week 5 instead of the back-end of the season. And yet, the 2-5 Philadelphia Eagles and 1-4-1 Washington Commanders were not flexed out this weekend, even though there are far more compelling and flex-worthy games on the Week 8 Sunday schedule. Is this just another case of NFC East bias? Well, it’s a little more complicated than that, and it’s largely the NFL’s own doing.

Eagles-Commanders Preview: Will Saquon Barkley Tough It Out? SHOULD He? – PHLY Eagles Podcast

Saquon Barkley returned the practice field just in time to put his status in play for the Eagles’ road matchup against the Washington Commanders on Sunday night. EJ Smith is joined by Deniz Selman and Brandon Lee Gowton to discuss whether the star running back should push through the hamstring and back injury he entered the week dealing with, whether Jeremiah Trotter Jr. should take over for Jihaad Campbell, and how this year’s team compares to previous lost Eagles seasons.

In Roob’s Observations: Has the league figured out Vic Fangio? – NBCSP

COULD HOWIE DRAFT A QUARTERBACK? As it stands now the Eagles would have the sixth pick in next year’s draft, and they’ve only drafted that high twice in the last 25 years, taking Lane Johnson fourth in 2013 and Carson Wentz second in 2016. Before that you go back to Corey Simon sixth in 2000 and Donovan McNabb second in 1999. Before that? Kenny Jackson fourth in 1984. So four top-6 picks in the last 42 years. What direction would Howie Roseman go if the Eagles draft that high? We can rule out receiver, running back, tight end, linebacker, corner or safety, which leaves trenches and quarterback. Edge or o-line never surprises you with Howie, but you don’t get many opportunities to draft top-10 quarterbacks, and if the Eagles are concerned with Jalen Hurts’ long-term health, and it’s something they won’t talk about, quarterback makes a lot of sense. You probably wouldn’t get Oklahoma State’s Drew Mestemaker at 6, but C.J. Carr of Notre Dame and Darian Mensah of Miami are in play if there is concern about Hurts being healthy enough to play in 2027 and beyond. Howie has drafted three quarterbacks in the first three rounds as a GM, and all three played a key role on a Super Bowl championship. Nick Foles and Jalen Hurts were Super Bowl MVPs and Carson Wentz went 11-2 before getting hurt in 2017. There is no No. 1 seed without him. It’s hard to imagine having to move on from a Super Bowl-MVP quarterback at 28 years old, but there are so many unknowns with his condition and treatment that it’s possible. Hurts’ contract status only complicates matters because with limited guarantees beyond this year it’s hard to imagine him playing for the Eagles in 2027 without a new or re-worked contract. But are the Eagles ready to give him a new deal when he’ll miss most of this year after a middling five games? So many questions and not a lot of answers.

NFL Week 8 fantasy sleepers: QB Sam Darnold, RB Rico Dowdle, WR Ja’Kobi Lane among upside plays – NFL.com

Scary Terry McLaurin can’t frighten defenses anymore after his season-ending knee injury, so someone in Washington has to step up and assume his mantle. There’s plenty of reason to believe it’ll be Okonkwo. Since Jayden Daniels’ return from injury in Week 5, Okonkwo leads the Commanders with 61 routes, 13 targets, 11 catches and 129 yards. Two of his six double-digit fantasy games since the start of last season came in his last two outings. Philadelphia’s defense might have been nightmare fuel for the rest of the NFC East over the last few years, but that reign of terror could be coming to a close with five straight losses punctuated by a home splattering last Monday night. I didn’t see a lot of fight in that outing with a whopping 0.34 EPA per dropback allowed, the unit’s worst performance under coordinator Vic Fangio. Daniels, Okonkwo and the Washington offense should be the scary ones under the lights in Landover.

The Best Bets of NFL Week 8 – The Ringer

There’s still a lot of talent on this defense, but the edge rushers are all battling injuries. Nolan Smith didn’t play Monday, and Jalyx Hunt and Jonathan Greenard look compromised. Cooper DeJean and Jalen Carter look considerably worse than they’ve been in past seasons, and Vic Fangio hasn’t shown a willingness to bring extra pressure. There are more holes in this defense than its still great defensive market rating would suggest. The market opened Washington as a 4.5-point favorite at home. It has a massive rest advantage and should be much healthier coming off the bye. This is the fifth time that an Eagles fade has made it into this column, and we’re looking to make it a clean 5-0 (after correct calls against Tennessee, Chicago, Los Angeles, and Dallas). The Eagles haven’t hit rock bottom yet, but Monday night’s lackluster defensive effort suggests that it’s nearing. Bet: Commanders –5.5 (–110)

How many trades will Eagles make — if they can break their losing streak?: Eagles-Commanders questions – The Athletic

Berman: My guess is two or three trades. I think Moro Ojomo and Riq Woolen will be moved. I’ll put Goedert as the third. I don’t think a Barkley or Zack Baun blockbuster is the direction they go. Landon Dickerson is the player with term on his contract that I’d watch closely. Although, as you outlined, is it worth eating $27.2 million for a Day 3 pick? I’d focus more closely on the expiring contracts and think the Eagles will try to maximize those returns. That could also include small deals for less-prominent players on expiring contracts. Knowing Roseman, a young player on a cost-controlled contract could always come in as a way of building for beyond this season. (That wouldn’t make the Eagles buyers as much as builders.) But I don’t think the Eagles will make moves with 2026 in mind. Don’t count me as someone who gets caught up in the compensatory pick strategy. That’s more applicable when the team is a contender in the second half of the season. Unless the Eagles think they’re contenders, it makes more sense to get a guaranteed return than the theoretical return with a compensatory pick.

Spadaro: Game Preview at Commanders, 6 storylines to follow – PhiladelphiaEagles.com

Philadelphia’s run defense is in the spotlight. Following a tough outing on Monday night against Dallas, how does the run defense respond? The Commanders average 125.2 rushing yards per game, so they know how to get it done and they do it with Daniels and a committee in the backfield. There isn’t much more to say here. The challenge is right there in front of the defense. It’s a reasonable expectation that the Commanders will come out early and try to establish the ground game.

The Vet was almost a dome. Would public sentiment for the next Eagles stadium be different if it had been? – Inquirer

“We would have to take the time to find out what the public wants,” he said. “We would have to look into it long and hard. Conceivably, a permanent dome could bring another white elephant to Philadelphia.” Sixty years later, the city is on the precipice of another stadium debate. The Eagles are in what Jeffrey Lurie earlier this year called their “exploratory research” phase when it comes to their future home. They could renovate the 23-year-old Lincoln Financial Field, or they could build a new stadium altogether. The Eagles’ lease at the Linc does not expire until 2032, but a discussion about the future certainly will play out long before then. There will be plenty of D’Ortonas, probably as many devil’s advocates like Snider, and others like the 1966 editorial staff of The Inquirer, who wrote that “there is still something to be said for fresh air and sunshine.” One present-day reader commented on a recent Inquirer story about why the Eagles would be paying close attention to Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London and said “Philadelphia should pass a law that Eagles home games must be played outside.” In response to a July article that said extreme weather during the World Cup at Lincoln Financial Field would be useful data to Lurie that, a reader emailed that “the blue collar element of Philly wants outdoor football.”

Colts willing to trade RB Jonathan Taylor, per report – Big Blue View

The Indianapolis Colts are now willing to trade star running back Jonathan Taylor, per a report from Adam Schefter of ESPN. Schefter adds in his report that the New York Giants are among the teams thought to have at least “some level of interest” in trading for Taylor. Schefter also lists the Seattle Seahawks, Denver Broncos, Minnesota Vikings, Green Bay Packers as teams believed to be interested in trading for Taylor. It’s no secret that while new Giants head coach John Harbaugh likes the trio of Cam Skattebo, Tyrone Tracy, and Devin Singletary, he has coveted a “bellcow” running back.

Cowboys vs Cardinals: 3 causes for concern in Week 8 – Blogging The Boys

3) The Cardinals problem. It’s fairly hard to believe, but the Arizona Cardinals may be Dallas’ toughest matchup over the course of the last decade plus. Since 2008, the Cowboys are a shocking 1-8 in their last nine matchups against the Cardinals, with four of those losses coming at home. Since that 2008 campaign in which they started their winning ways against Dallas, the Cardinals have a 134-164-2 regular season record as a team. Arizona has rarely been one of the better teams in the league, but they always seem to find a way to beat the Cowboys, regardless of how their season is going. Year-to-year team trends don’t mean much in the NFL, but it’s hard not to be concerned about Dallas’ struggles against the Cardinals. This game feels eerily similar to the Week 9 matchup between the two teams last season. Arizona won that game 27-17 as the Cowboys looked unprepared and undisciplined. The Cowboys have a big-time Cardinals problem that they’ll look to put to rest on Sunday.

Patriots vs. Dolphins Friday injury report: A.J. Brown among New England’s questionable for Week 8 – Pats Pulpit

The New England Patriots will wait for the weekend before making a final call on No. 1. A.J. Brown headlines the team’s questionable to face the Miami Dolphins after going from a limited participant to missing consecutive practices to end AFC East prep. The three-time All-Pro wide receiver is dealing with a knee issue that flared up while also working back from the high ankle sprain that sent him to injured reserve in September. “His status is questionable, like some other players,” head coach Mike Vrabel told reporters on Friday. “We’ll see how he comes in tomorrow and we’ll make a decision.”

item.title: Draft prospects for the NY Giants in Week 9 of college football
item.description: Which 2027 NFL Draft prospects should you be watching in Week 9 of the 2026 college football season?
item.content:encoded:
Good morning New York Giants fans! Happy Saturday and welcome to Week 9 of the 2026 College Football Season.

The Giants are on their bye week this week and are guaranteed to control the NFC East regardless of what happens, so we’re all free to sit back and simply enjoy a weekend of football without stakes

As usual, we’re using college football and the NFL Draft as a lens through which to look at the New York Giants. In particular, we’re going to look at the Giants’ needs as we perceive them, and focus on players who could fit those needs.

Texas Tech vs. Arizona

ESPN – Noon

Don’t look now, but Arizona is quietly making noise and could force their way into the College Football Playoffs. Texas Tech is more highly regarded right now, but Arizona is a fun team to watch. Keep an eye on freshman linebacker Dash Fifita, younger brother of Arizona QB Noah Fifita. Dash is coming off a game against Iowa State with 2.5 tackles for a loss and 2.0 sacks… At 5-foot-7, 190 pounds. He won’t be draft eligible for two more years and might not be a draftable prospect due to his size, but he’s fun.

For our purposes, however, I want to turn to the Texas Tech defense.

Player spotlight: A.J. Holmes Jr. (iDL, Texas Tech)

Holmes jr. transferred to Texas Tech a year ago, and was a productive member of that disruptive defensive front which carried them into the playoffs.

He’s having a fantastic year as “The Guy” on Texas Tech’s defensive line. So far he has 6.5 tackles for a loss and 6.5 sacks (leads the Big 12) though 7 games, as well as 23 total tackles and a forced fumble. Holmes Jr. is listed at 6-foot-3, 300 pounds, but plays with solid leverage and anchor, as well as impressive explosiveness and power. He excels at firing out of his stance and using heavy hands to rock blockers backward before shedding and using his agility and burst to make a play on the ball. He would likely be best in a 1-gap system at the next level, and could fit the Giants as a 3 or 5-technique depending on their personnel package.

As things stand now, Holmes Jr. is probably a second round pick, but he could work his way into the “1st – 2nd” range if he continues to produce as a disruptor.

(8) BYU vs. Arizona State

Fox – 3:30 p.m.

Most of the nation will be watching BYU to see if they can rebound after their 39-31 loss to UCF a week ago. BYU catapulted themselves into the national spotlight and the Playoff conversation with their upset win over Notre Dame two weeks ago, but couldn’t avoid the letdown game the following week.

For our purposes, however, we’ll be taking a look at the Sundevils. Arizona State has produced some interesting prospects over the last couple years, notably Cam Skattebo, WR Jordan Tyson, and now QB Sam Leavitt (currently at LSU). We’re going to stick to the offensive side of the ball and one of the fastest risers in recent weeks.

Player spotlight: Reed Harris (WR, Arizona State)

Both Harris and fellow WR Omario Miller could be of interest to the Giants, and both could be solid Day 2 picks. We’re going to focus on Harris, because he’s having a better year and his physical profile could be more appealing to the Giants. Harris is a transfer from Boston College and is an imposing presence on the field. He’s listed at 6-foot-5, 220 pounds and looks every bit of it. He appears to have solid speed and agility for a big receiver and plays with plenty of power. He has a massive catch radius as well as the ability to drag defenders as a ball carrier.

There would likely be some overlap between Harris and Malachi Fields, however redundancy isn’t necessarily a bad thing. The Giants have increasingly used Malik Nabers in the slot and he’s responded well, getting nearly as many yards from the slot as out wide, despite having far fewer snaps as a slot receiver. Adding a second big wide receiver could allow the Giants to use Nabers as a slot receiver even more often, or create size mismatches with smaller corners.

North Carolina vs. (1) Miami

ABC – 7:30 p.m.

We’re checking in on the ACC in the evening slate. The matchups between Ohio State and USC or Texas and Mississippi State may be more compelling, but the Hurricanes have a number of defensive players that could interest the Giants. Likewise, QB Darian Mensah could be one of the linchpins early in the draft, and sophomore WR Malachi Toney is simply a human highlight reel.

Player Spotlight: Justin Scott (iDL, Miami)

The Giants might not want to spend a first round pick on a defensive tackle — or the board may not line up for them even if they do. But, as noted up above, this is shaping up to be an impressively deep defensive tackle class. We’ve already talked about Miami defensive tackle Ahmad Moten, and his teammate is a high-upside player as well.

Scott has a versatile frame at 6-foot-4, 305 pounds with enough length and strength to play any gap alignment in an even or odd front. He boasts an explosive first step and should be a dangerous gap-shooter in a one-gap defense, while also having a powerful lower body to take on blockers in the run game. In addition to great explosiveness and power, he also has the kind of wide-open motor and competitive toughness we’ve come to expect from this Miami defense. That combination should appeal to the Giants’ coaching staff, and Scott could easily step into Shelby Harris’ spot as a 3, 4i, or 5-technique.

There’s currently some speculation that Scott could work his way into the first round conversation thanks to his traits. However, this could be a very deep defensive tackle class and there are prospects with similarly impressive traits who also have significant production to their name. As of this writing, Scott has 21 tackles but only 1.0 tackle for a loss and 0 sacks on the season. Unlike many of the defensive tackles the Giants have drafted lately, Scott is still young and won’t turn 21 until January. It’s possible that he could slide in a deep class and be available to the Giants somewhere in the second round.

item.title: The importance of during the Saints’ bye week
item.description: The Saints have to come out of this bye week looking like a different team
item.content:encoded:
This bye week for the New Orleans Saints is the most important one in the current era of the franchise.

At a time when this team entered the season with so much hope and promise, built on how last season ended, the trust of the fan base is beginning to wane.

The team showed flashes of a promising future: a young head coach with previous success as an offensive coordinator, a rookie quarterback who appeared to be a budding superstar, two solid young offensive tackles who looked to be the bookends of what should have been a competent offensive line, and a front office that finally seemed to be turning the page and getting its act together.

After the first half of the season, all of that appears to have been misjudged.

Now, this team sits with only two wins, the offense that seems lost, and two recent draft classes that are beginning to look like major whiffs. The head coach can’t seem to put together an offensive game plan that allows the team to start games effectively and sustain success for an entire contest.

So, this bye week means a lot.

As things currently stand, the Saints are still on the cusp of competing for a very weak division. However, if they come out of this bye week with the same offensive issues, an inability to run the football, a team that has managed to score no more than six total first-quarter points all season, and consistent problems with blocking up front, then the statement made by the owner two weeks ago, which still looms over this team like a cloud, will only ring hollow in the ears of the Who Dat Nation faithful.

If the Saints come out of this bye week without making changes to the coaching staff, they will absolutely have to demonstrate meaningful changes on the field.

And if they don’t, trust will be broken, and apathy will begin to set in.

The last thing any professional sports franchise should want is for its fan base to become apathetic toward the team.

At least frustration stems from passion, and that passion can drive change and progress. Apathy, on the other hand, only leads to the team being ignored and fans finding better ways to spend their time and, most importantly, their money.

This upcoming week will be incredibly important, and the results of the work, sacrifice, and development of this roster and coaching staff will be evident from the opening moments of the next game.

Hope is gone. Faith is low. Trust is slipping away.

The Saints must approach this bye week with a sense of urgency and make the necessary changes to restore confidence in this team and organization.

item.title: College football’s top Cowboys draft targets in Week 9
item.description: What CFB game are you most looking forward to?﻿
item.content:encoded:
We are getting deep into the college football season as we continue our look at possible draft targets for the Dallas Cowboys in 2027.

Florida vs. Georgia

Florida and Georgia meet in Atlanta with the Gators’ ground game facing one of its most revealing tests. Georgia has allowed only 91 rushing yards per game, while Florida has built much of its offense around Jadan Baugh. That puts Baugh and Bulldogs linebacker Chris Cole at the center of the matchup.

Florida: Jadan Baugh, running back

Baugh has carried the Florida offense through seven games, rushing 135 times for 763 yards and 13 touchdowns. He has the frame of a volume runner, but his game contains more than straightforward power. He can make the first defender miss and accelerate through the opening before the pursuit closes. Florida can use him in gap concepts or zone runs without changing the identity of the offense.

His contact balance is the trait that consistently stands out. Baugh absorbs glancing hits and keeps his feet through congestion. He’s generated some impressive yards after contact and missed tackles this season, illustrating how often he creates additional yardage without perfect blocking. His lower-body strength makes him dependable in short-yardage situations, but he also has enough lateral quickness to cut away from penetration and enough speed to punish a defense once he reaches the second level.

Why The Cowboys Care

We all know what Javonte Williams is but the depth chart behind him does not offer the same certainty going into next year. Baugh could enter as a physical second option, handle pass protection and receiving responsibilities, and eventually develop into the primary back. His ability to create after contact would also help an offense that cannot assume every rushing lane will be clean.

Dallas should not chase Baugh if he rises into the opening round, but he becomes a serious consideration if he remains available in the Cowboys’ Day 2 range.

Georgia: Chris Cole, linebacker

Cole is one of the defenders most directly responsible for limiting Baugh so we get a game here where we can directly watch both players on our list face off against each other and battle it out. Cole has recorded 40 tackles, 8.5 tackles for loss, 2.5 sacks, and three pass breakups this season after producing 59 tackles, seven tackles for loss and 4.5 sacks in 2025. Georgia uses his length and movement skills in several ways, allowing him to run with a tight end, close on a back in the flat, blitz through an interior gap or rush from the edge.

His coverage ability separates him from many linebackers in this class, and with the way the linebacker position is evolving this makes him an exciting player. Cole reads releases quickly, has the range to carry routes into space and uses his length. He earned an 88.9 PFF coverage grade last season and showed the broader value of his game against Alabama, finishing with eight tackles, 2.5 tackles for loss, a sack and two pass breakups. That combination suggests a three-down role rather than a player who must leave the field in passing situations.

Why The Cowboys Care

Jaishawn Barham has emerged as an intriguing piece of the Dallas defense, but the long-term linebacker picture stays questionable. DeMarvion Overshown’s availability has been difficult to project, and the defense still needs players who can handle coverage assignments without sacrificing pressure ability. Cole could play the weak side, match running backs and tight ends, and become another movable piece for Christian Parker.

His versatility would be especially useful beside Barham. Dallas could let Barham attack downhill while Cole ranges in space.

Arizona vs. Texas Tech

Arizona brings a five-game winning streak and one of the country’s most efficient passing attacks to Lubbock. Texas Tech counters with a disruptive defensive front led by A.J. Holmes Jr. The Wildcats’ protection will be central to the result, giving veteran right tackle Tristan Bounds a valuable opportunity against a front that creates pressure from multiple alignments and through coordinated movement.

Arizona: Tristan Bounds, offensive tackle

Bounds is difficult to miss at 6-foot-8 and 320 pounds. The sixth-year senior began his career at Michigan and started eight games at right tackle for Arizona in 2025 before a season-ending injury. He returned this year and has allowed eight pressures but no sacks across 462 snaps, earning a 78.2 pass-blocking grade from PFF.

His length gives him an enormous margin in pass protection. Bounds can engage an edge rusher before the defender reaches his chest and widen the path to the quarterback. He is patient enough to avoid opening the inside lane too early, and when his base is set he has the mass to absorb power. Those traits make him particularly effective when Arizona asks him to protect a defined pocket and give its passing game time to work downfield.

Why The Cowboys Care

Dallas needs a clearer long-term answer at swing tackle and more competition on the right side. Bounds has the length and pass-protection foundation to compete for a reserve role while the Cowboys coaches work on his pad level, footwork and play strength.

His current projection is closer to Day 3 than the top of the draft. That makes this game especially important. If Bounds handles an active Texas Tech front, he can begin to establish himself as a draftable developmental tackle rather than simply an experienced college starter. 

Texas Tech: A.J. Holmes Jr., defensive tackle

Holmes has been one of the most productive interior defenders in college football this seasons. He’s generated 32 pressures and seven sacks this season, leading all FBS defensive tackles in pressures while ranking near the top of the position in pass-rush grade. That production follows an All-America 2025 season in which he recorded 38 tackles, nine tackles for loss and 4.5 sacks.

He wins with quickness, leverage and active hands. Holmes fires into gaps before guards can establish their base and uses lateral movement to attack an edge or redirect when the quarterback moves. His first step creates immediate stress for protection schemes, and he works well within stunts because he can penetrate or wrap into the newly opened lane quickly. He is not merely collecting cleanup sacks, his pressure total reflects how frequently he disturbs the pocket.

Why The Cowboys Care

Sure, Dallas has Quinnen Williams and Kenny Clark, but succession planning is necessary at a position that’s strong on a defense that’s still building. L.T. Overton offers a young building block, yet the defense still needs another interior lineman who can collapse the pocket and keep the veteran starters from carrying an excessive snap load.

Holmes could enter as the second-wave three-technique defender, contribute on passing downs and develop behind Williams and Clark who can mentor him to become the next cornerstone on the inside. His quickness would fit the movement and pressure concepts Parker can build around the front, while his experience should help him earn rotational snaps sooner than a raw developmental tackle.

item.title: Previewing the New York Jets’ opposition: Las Vegas Raiders
item.description: The Jets are home to take on the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday
item.content:encoded:
The Jets and Raiders represent two franchises that have been trying to rebuild for a long time, without much success. Having picked first and second in the 2026 NFL draft, the teams meet on Sunday with each trying desperately not to fall out of contention yet again. While the Jets could easily be better than their current 2-5 record, the Raiders stand 3-4 having won their first three only to then lose four straight.

When these teams last met, in 2023, Las Vegas beat the Jets 16-12 in a frustrating game that dropped the Jets below .500. Whoever loses this one will be similarly frustrated.

Let’s break down the Raiders’ roster going position by position:

Quarterbacks

The Raiders got rid of Geno Smith during the offseason and replaced him with someone even older, the 38-year old Kirk Cousins. So far, Cousins is off to a productive start and the Raiders have the number four passing game in the NFL as he leads the league with 16 touchdown passes.

However, while the Raiders have been marching up and down the field and are 2nd in the league in terms of red zone visits, they are down in 29th for touchdown conversion percentage in the red zone. They were 1-for-5 down there in Sunday’s loss to the Rams.

Of course, the biggest quarterback story for the Raiders is currently on ice, as the number one overall pick Fernando Mendoza won’t get a chance to show the Jets what they missed out on unless Cousins is hurt or benched during Sunday’s game. His first start probably isn’t too far away though, and he did complete six of eight passes in garbage time action so far this season.

The number three is Aidan O’Connell, who beat the Jets as a rookie in the aforementioned 2023 game.

Offensive Line

The Raiders’ offensive line was awful last year, although two of the players they got rid of – Dylan Parham and Jordan Meredith – are actually faring quite well with the Jets.

Former Raven Tyler Linderbaum was brought in at center to stabilize things, signing a massive $81 million deal. The jury is still out on this deal because, while the offensive line is definitely improved, his own performance has been somewhat underwhelming. He leads the team with five offensive penalties in seven games.

The Raiders also brought in Spencer Burford on a low-cost one-year deal and he’s currently starting at left guard. Burford is best known for blowing a costly assignment in overtime during the 49ers’ recent Super Bowl loss.

The other three players listed as starters are all returning from last year’s group: Kolton Miller at left tackle, DJ Glaze at right tackle and Jackson Powers-Johnson at right guard. However, Powers-Johnson was recently benched for Caleb Rogers with the suggestion being that he doesn’t fit the system and could be traded at the deadline. He is also listed as questionable having missed practice time due to a back issue.

Glaze led the team in offensive snaps last year, as the one constant on a line that kept changing personnel. Miller is the team’s highest paid offensive player, but has given up a team-high four sacks.

The rest of the bench comprises guard Bryce Cabeldue, tackle Charles Grant and third round rookie guard Trey Zuhn III. Grant was a third round pick who had one start as a rookie last season but Cabeldue and Zuhn have played less than 50 offensive snaps between them in regular season action. Zuhn sees some time as a sixth lineman in jumbo packages, though.

Running Backs

Last year’s top pick Ashton Jeanty continues to see a lot of the ball and rack up production by volume even though he hasn’t been all that effective with a 3.1 yards per carry average. Having come within 25 yards of a thousand-yard season as a rookie, he’s ramped up his passing game production this year and has accounted for 640 yards from scrimmage with four total touchdowns.

Jeanty made headlines during the week when he suggested that unnamed Jets players didn’t like to tackle. That was ironic given that he is 25th out of 26 qualifying backs in terms of forced missed tackles so far this season according to Pro Football Focus.

Fourth round rookie Mike Washington Jr. has shown some early promise in a reserve role, though, as he is averaging almost five yards per carry.

Dylan Laube is the number three back and Connor Heyward is listed as the fullback, although he will also line up at tight end.

Pass catchers

The Raiders’ best pass catching weapon is pro bowler Brock Bowers. The tight end missed two games but is still tied with Jeanty for the team lead in receptions on 31, for 455 yards and three scores. His fellow tight end Michael Mayer also has 31 catches.

Leading the team in receiving yards and touchdown receptions, though, is Tre Tucker with 474 yards and four scores.

No other Raiders wideout has double figures in catches, although Cody White has made his eight catches count, with three of them being touchdowns.

Jalen Nailor is the other starter along with Tucker, but has just 75 yards on eight catches for the season. Last year’s second round pick, Jack Bech, would presumably be playing a significant role if he weren’t on injured reserve, though, and he has been practicing this week so he may be about to return. His official game status is questionable.

Dont’e Thornton, Malik Benson and Dareke Young are also on the roster at wideout and Ian Thomas is the number three tight end. Benson was drafted in the sixth round in April.

Defensive Line

As ever, the Raiders’ biggest threat on either side of the ball is all-pro defensive end Maxx Crosby. However, it’s the other two edges in the Raiders’ three man rotation – Malcolm Koonce and Kwity Paye – who are tied for the team lead on three sacks each. Crosby certainly hasn’t been slacking, though. His 16 quarterback hits are more than twice as many as any other player on the team.

At defensive tackle, Adam Butler and Tonka Hemingway are listed as the starters. However, ex-Jet Folorunso Fatukasi has actually started all seven games.

With third round pick Keyron Crawford on injured reserve, depth on the edge comes from Patrick Johnson, although he’s out of Sunday’s game with a stinger. Thomas Booker and JJ Pegues provide further depth inside.

Linebackers

The Raiders signed linebacker Nakobe Dean to a $12 million per year contract in the offseason and he’s been a settling influence on the defense in the same way Linderbaum was supposed to be for the offense. Dean is tied for the league lead with three forced fumbles and has 68 tackles, 1.5 sacks and an interception.

The other starter at linebacker is former first round pick Quay Walker, who has a team-high five tackles for loss, while Tommy Eichenberg sees action in base packages.

Cody Lindenberg and Segun Olubi provide depth off the bench. Olubi started two games for the Colts back in 2023.

Defensive Backs

The Raiders’ 3-0 start was significantly influenced by fifth round rookie Hezekiah Masses, who intercepted three passes in the first three games. However, since that time, Masses has found himself back in a reserve role as he has given up four touchdowns and five defensive penalties with the defense now statistically one of the league’s worst.

Eric Stokes, who signed a three-year, $30 million extension during the offseason and Darien Porter are now starting on the outside after Porter had previously seen his starting role taken away by Masses. In addition, Taron Johnson is one of the most reliable slot specialists in the league.

At safety, the Raiders drafted Treydan Stukes in the second round and he’s been starting alongside veteran Jeremy Chinn. Isaiah Pola-Mao sees time in three-safety sets.

The Raiders also drafted Jermod McCoy and Dalton Johnson in the middle rounds to add some depth at corner. Cornerback Darrell Luter is also on the roster, as is safety Tristin McCollum.

Special Teams

On special teams, former pro bowler AJ Cole is still a solid punter, who is currently second in the NFL for gross average. Kicker Matt Gay is also solid, with just two misses on the season.

Laube, who had a 53-yard runback earlier this year, is the main kickoff returner and backs up Benson on punt returns. Young also gets work on kick returns, in addition to being the team’s primary gunner in punt coverage.

Their linebackers are productive in kick coverage as Lindenberg and Olubi are tied for the team lead with eight special teams tackles. Eichenberg was fourth in the league with 21 last season.

item.title: Packers’ Micah Parsons reportedly eyeing Week 12 return for Thanksgiving Eve game against Rams
item.description: Parsons has been out since suffering a torn ACL in Week 15 last season.
item.content:encoded:
Micah Parsons is reportedly targeting Nov. 25 as his return to the Green Bay Packers lineup, according to NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport.

The linebacker has not played since suffering a torn ACL in Week 15 last season. In August, he said it was "very realistic" he could return in Week 6, but that date has come and come and now Green Bay’s Thanksgiving Eve game against the Los Angeles Rams appears to be more realistic.

"It's just about me making sure I have all the small things fixed first," Parsons said earlier this month on his "The Edge" podcast. "What a lot of people don't figure out is it's not just the ACL. It's like, why did the ACL happen? What was weak? Because it all works together. It's a chain. And throughout the history of ACL, they notice if you come back early, there tends to be an overcompensation injury on the other side. ... We just gonna make sure everything is right before."

There is a return plan in place with Week 12 being the goal. Parsons is expected to return to practice this week and take part in individual drills. The following week he will participate in team drills, barring a setback. The 5-3 Packers have their bye week in Week 11, allowing an extra week of recovery and work before Parsons could potentially return to the field.

Parsons, who was acquired by the Packers in Aug. 2025 from the Dallas Cowboys, recorded 12.5 sacks, 41 total tackles and two forced fumbles over 14 games before suffering the injury.

item.title: Josh Jacobs could be on thin ice in Green Bay
item.description: Throughout his off-field incident that resulted in a no-contest plea to misdemeanor battery, the Packers have remained steadfast in their support of running back Josh Jacobs.
item.content:encoded:
Throughout his off-field incident that resulted in a no-contest plea to misdemeanor battery, the Packers have remained steadfast in their support of running back Josh Jacobs.

That could now be changing.

The persistent presence of the Packers as one of the teams that have expressed some degree of interest in trading for Colts running back Jonathan Taylor suggests that they've at least pondered the possibility of swapping out Jacobs for Taylor.

Recent developments don't help Jacobs's cause.

Beyond the handcuff celebration that Jacobs tried to say wasn’t a handcuff celebration (but that video of the full celebration suggests was a handcuff celebration), Friday's release of police records indicating that at least three other women have accused Jacobs of domestic violence could shake the team's apparent resolve to keep him.

Throw in the fact that Jacobs is averaging 2.3 yards per carry in his two games back from a six-game stint on paid leave — including 1.9 yards per carry against the worst run defense in the league entering Thursday night's game — and it's possible that the Packers will realize that Jacobs is no longer good enough to justify a stubborn circling of the wagons.

Cutting Jacobs would raise the issue of termination pay as to the balance of his $10.2 million salary, and it would short-circuit the team's ability to seek partial repayment of signing-bonus money if/when (when) he's eventually suspended under the Personal Conduct Policy. For now, we won't delve into the full extent of the niceties of Article 30 of the CBA; at a minimum, the Packers would have some potential arguments aimed at cutting off his right to any termination pay.

Even if the Packers ultimately are on the hook for termination pay, it's a sunk cost. The question is whether they want to keep him on the team, in light of recent developments.

Again, they've been linked in multiple reports from ESPNFL to a trade for Jonathan Taylor. That alone is substantial evidence that they're considering a future without Jacobs that could begin sooner rather than later.

item.title: Eagles opposing player to stop, Week 8 edition
item.description: Philadelphia’s struggling defense will be tested by the Commanders’ third-year QB.
item.content:encoded:
The Eagles are a mess. They are the unproud owners of a five-game losing skid, the longest losing streak in the NFC and currently the second-longest streak in the NFL behind the winless Los Angeles Chargers. The Eagles sit in third place in the hapless NFC East, not that it is any great distinction, one game up on their next opponent, the one-win Washington Commanders, this Sunday night on national TV.

If you’re wondering how low the Eagles can go, they are 5.5-point underdogs against the one-win Commanders, who even with one victory hold a larger upside this season than the sinking, listless Eagles.

The Eagles are currently ranked 31st in offense, averaging 264.9 yards a game, and 29th in scoring, averaging an NFC-low 18.1 points a game. Defensively, the Eagles are not much better, ranked No. 27 in the NFL, giving up an average of 371.3 yards a game, and 25 points a game.   

The Eagles are coming off their worst performance of the season, giving up a season-high 416 total yards that translated into a season-high 38 points in the 38-21 to the Dallas Cowboys on Monday night.

One weapon the Commanders have that the Eagles do not have is Jayden Daniels, despite the fact that he is 0-7-1 in his last eight starts and will be without Eagle killer Terry McLaurin, out for the season after surgery on Friday to repair the torn patellar tendon in his left knee. Even without McLaurin, the Commanders will be the better team.

Defensive tackles Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis were awful against Dallas. They were nowhere to be found. They had no quarterback pressures and were knocked off the ball the whole night. The Cowboys ran 65 plays and the vaunted Eagles’ defense had zero tackles for a loss. Carter, the highest paid defensive tackle in the NFL, ran from adversity and declined to talk to the media after the game and continued with his denial of putting out a maximum effort against Dallas this week leading into the Washington game.

At least Eagles’ defensive coordinator Vic Fangio was accountable—as he should have been. When asked about a lack of effort, Fangio denied seeing any lack of effort, although he did say, “I didn’t do a good enough job coaching. We didn’t play the run, obviously, well enough. When you do that, it kind of affects everything. I didn’t have them ready to do that the way we need to. We just didn’t play it well.”

Numerous sources in and around the Eagles have told Bleeding Green Nation recently that they still trust and believe in Nick Sirianni and Fangio. That the pair still have the locker room. They still somehow believe that Sirianni and Fangio can turn around this disaster, because they have done it before. That they still have faith the Eagles will be playing in vital November and December games. But where there was once unbending support for learning-on-the-job offensive coordinator Sean Mannion and offensive line coach Chris Kuper may be bending. It has changed to doubt as the Eagles keep sinking.

item.title: Dolphins claim Jamree Kromah in edge rusher shake up
item.description: The Miami Dolphins added an edge rusher on Saturday.
item.content:encoded:
The Miami Dolphins claimed Jamree Kromah off waivers on Saturday, adding the former Chicago Bears edge rusher to the team’s 53-man active roster. To make roster space, the Dolphins waived edge rusher Robert Beal, Jr.

Kromah began his NFL career as an undrafted free agent whom the Bears signed in 2024. He began his rookie year on Chicago’s practice squad before signing with the New England Patriots shortly after the start of 2024. He was waived a monthly later, returning to the Bears’ practice squad. He then spent 2025 on Chicago’s practice squad before making it to the active roster for 2026. He was waived this week after the Bears acquired defensive tackle Jeffrey Simmons in a trade.

He has appeared in two games, recording two tackles.

Beal played in two games with the Dolphins this season, his first in Miami after three seasons with the San Francisco 49ers. He has one tackle.

Kromah joins Chop Robinson, Josh Uche, Malik Herring, and Rodney McGraw as Miami’s edge rushers.

The Dolphins face the New England Patriots on Sunday. Kickoff is set for 4:25 p.m. Eastern.

item.title: John Harbaugh violated norms, called Titans ownership about Jeffery Simmons
item.description: Let’s talk about what that says about Harbaugh and the Giants.
item.content:encoded:
New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh took the extraordinary step of calling Tennessee Titans ownership directly in an effort to acquire star defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons, according to a startling report from Jonathan Jones of The Athletic.

Per Jones, that breaks with “traditional NFL trade-talk norms” where general managers deal directly with each other.

Jones reported that Harbaugh contacted Titans owner Amy Adams Strunk after Giants GM Joe Schoen had been told by Titans GM Mike Borgonzi that Simmons, a 29-year-old four-time Pro Bowler and 2025 First-Team All-Pro, would not be traded. Strunk apparently gave Harbaugh the same message.

That obviously changed when the Chicago Bears made a Godfather offer to the Titans of two first-round and a fourth-round draft pick.

Per Jones, one GM said Harbaugh’s call to Strunk “violates a code amongst primary football decision-makers, that they will only deal with each other.”

Valentine’s View

Whether Harbaugh violated NFL traditions or not, the move tells you a couple of things about the Giants.

  1. This is clearly Harbaugh’s show. We have told you that before, but this is absolutely evidence that Harbaugh is front-and-center in every major decision, and that he will do whatever he believes necessary to get something done. Even if that steps on toes.
  2. The Giants are clearly intent upon seizing the opportunity they have in the NFC East. Forget building. Harbaugh wants the Giants to be the best they can be right now, and if there is a star player out there like Simmons or running back Jonathan Taylor who can help make that happen, the Giants will try to get it done.

Whether going for it right now is the correct approach, after the Giants have spent most of the last 15 years floundering you have to appreciate the boldness.

I think it is also important to note that Simmons and Taylor, who is now reportedly available, are players who would be more than short-term, 2026 upgrades.

One other note in terms of surrendering draft capital. Whether it is too early for a Jaxson Dart vs. J.J. McCarthy debate, the Giants clearly understand that if they spend draft capital now, they possess two desirable, 23-year-old quarterbacks and they can use one in the offseason to recoup premium draft picks.

item.title: Chiefs-Broncos: 5 questions with Mile High Report ahead of Week 8
item.description: We welcome Mile High Report for answers to five questions about Denver before Sunday Afternoon’s Week 8 matchup
item.content:encoded:
On Sunday, the Kansas City Chiefs face the Denver Broncos in the late afternoon slot of Week 8 games. We welcome Ian St. Clair of Mile High Report — our sister SBNation site covering the Broncos— for Five Questions with the Enemy.

Chiefs Kingdom, bring the noise to the SB Nation app!

Join fellow Chiefs fans to react to every explosive play and game-changing moment in real time.

  • Chat live throughout the game
  • Browse with fewer ads
  • Easily jump between communities
  • Enjoy faster commenting and posting

Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android.

Download the SB Nation app on your mobile device and join the Mile High Report community through Sunday’s game to get perspectives from both sides of the Week 8 matchup!

1.The Broncos lost 31-10 in Kansas City to open the season but have since won five of six games, including three consecutive victories entering this rematch. What has changed the most about Denver since that Week 1 loss?

The defense remembered how to tackle. In all seriousness, just put that horrible showing out of their minds and move on. However, getting humbled can also help level a person or team. The shellacking from the Chiefs was a great reminder that what happened last season has no bearing on the current one. So the Broncos better buckle up. And we’ve seen that in the last six games. The fact they’ve won five of six, with the gauntlet they had to start the season, is a testament to that.

2. Bo Nix produced two explosive touchdowns against Arizona, including a franchise-record 62-yard quarterback run, but he is still completing only 59.2% of his passes and averaging 182 passing yards per game. How would you evaluate Nix’s development through the first seven games?

Nix has been bad to start this season. He’s had his moments: the second half against the Jacksonville Jaguars and Los Angeles Rams, the two drives against the Seattle Seahawks in the first half (way more than Patrick Mahomes did against that defense), and then Sunday against the Cardinals. But he’s looked and played like a shell of himself to start this season. However, Nix played similarly to this in his rookie season and last season, so he has had sluggish starts. We’ll see if his performance against Arizona is the confidence builder that gets him and the offense clicking. Of course, all of this is easier to swallow when Denver is 5-2.

3. Seattle held the Chiefs to three points and limited Kenneth Walker III to 36 rushing yards last week. Denver leads the NFL with 21 sacks and could face a Kansas City offensive line starting backup tackles. How much of Seattle’s defensive blueprint can the Broncos reproduce in this rematch?

Honestly, just tackling Walker would be an improvement for the Broncos’ defense. But there’s no doubt defensive coordinator Vance Joseph and his assistants will look at what the Seahawks did and find ways to implement that in Sunday’s game plan. What will help Denver is the likely return of Patrick Surtain II, who has been out the last few games, and Jonathan Cooper, who missed the first game of the season. Something to keep an eye on, however, is Talanoa Hufanga has been ruled out, and now Brandon Jones showed up on the injury report with a hamstring. So potentially being down your starting safeties isn’t ideal. But Denver’s defense will be incredibly motivated on Sunday to replicate what Seattle did and make up for the Week 1 performance.

4. Jonah Coleman returned against Arizona and joined J.K. Dobbins and RJ Harvey in what has become a three-man backfield. Which Denver running back should the Chiefs consider the greatest threat entering Sunday’s game?

Running the ball, it’s Coleman. He runs much better than Dobbins right now and is a more dangerous threat with the ball. Payton said after the Cardinals win that Coleman needs more touches, so Coleman should get them on Sunday. As a receiving threat, that’s Harvey, as he showed on the 52-yard touchdown reception. So KC should prepare for more running back screens this Sunday.

5. Kansas City enters the game at 5-1, with Denver right behind at 5-2, making this an important early battle for control of the AFC West and positioning within the AFC playoff race. How do you see Sunday’s rematch playing out, including your final score prediction and how much control the winner will gain in the division race?

This is going to be a close game that will likely come down to the fourth quarter. Denver’s defense will play much better than that putrid showing to open the season. I also think Nix and the offense will build off last week against Arizona. The fact that the Broncos are playing at home gives them the edge, and they’ll get the 24-20 victory. That will put Denver in the lead for the AFC West, and with Kansas City’s upcoming schedule, puts it in a great spot to defend the division title.

item.title: Colts change course on Jonathan Taylor trade, insider says. What to know
item.description: The Colts fire sale is underway as owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon sets a new course for the franchise. RB Jonathan Taylor could be the next to go.
item.content:encoded:
The Indianapolis Colts have been the most active team in the NFL this season, at least away from the field.

Off to a 2-5 record on the field, the Colts have made major moves to set a new course for their future by firing GM Chris Ballard and by trading cornerstones Quenton Nelson – to the Seahawks – and DeForest Buckner – to the 49ers – for future draft assets as owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon commits to a rebuild.

The obvious question after those moves was whether Irsay-Gordon might be willing to also part with the face of the franchise in running back Jonathan Taylor. After initially reporting Oct. 27 that Irsay-Gordon did not want to trade Taylor, ESPN's NFL insider Adam Schefter said there has been a change of heart.

"The Indianapolis Colts now are open to trading star running back Jonathan Taylor," Schefter reported Saturday, Oct. 31. "Multiple teams have reached out to Indianapolis, and those talks are said to be active and ongoing, according to sources."

Taylor is off to an excellent start to the 2026 season with 587 yards on 140 carries in seven games. His eight rushing touchdowns are tied for the league lead, and his 83.9 yards per game rank fifth. He also has 17 catches for 178 receiving yards so far.

The former second-round pick in the 2020 NFL Draft has played for the Colts his entire career. In six and a half seasons in Indianapolis, Taylor has earned Pro Bowl nods three times and one first-team All-Pro recognition. Last year, Taylor ranked third in the NFL in scrimmage yards (1,963) and led the league in scrimmage touchdowns (20).

What Jonathan Taylor said about a possible trade

Taylor spoke to members of the media on Thursday, Oct. 29, and addressed some of the uncertainty that enshrouds his future in Indianapolis.

"I haven't heard anything," Taylor said. "I can't control that. Obviously, you guys know that I'm always proud to wear the horseshoe. I'm always proud to be here. ... But obviously, circumstances may cause otherwise. Hopefully that day may not come, but I can't control that."

Jonathan Taylor contract tradable despite extension

Indianapolis head coach Shane Steichen said on Wednesday, Oct. 28, that Taylor, a three-time Pro Bowler and this team’s most valuable asset right now, has not requested trade – even though WR Josh Downs has and despite the departures of Buckner and Nelson, who paved so many of Taylor’s comfy rush lanes.

But Taylor could and should be very much in play – even though he signed a two-year, $44 million extension on Aug. 6. A 27-year-old back at the peak of his powers – and with a pact that runs through the 2028 season – ought to be very enticing to contenders, especially those with lackluster ground games.

Taylor is surely the Colts’ best chance of recouping the 2027 first-rounder that Ballard surrendered last November to obtain CB Sauce Gardner from the New York Jets. And given Taylor would only create a very absorbable $10 million dead cap charge in 2027 – any acquiring team would be on the hook for the $34 million in total cash he’d be owed over the course of the 2027 and ’28 seasons – moving on from him should be an enticing and realistic option for the Colts, whose next championship window almost certainly won’t align with Taylor’s.

Jonathan Taylor trade landing spot: Best fits for Colts RB

Minnesota Vikings

The Vikings are the NFL's last unbeaten team, but they will need to upgrade their offense to keep it that way. They rank 28th league-wide in offensive EPA per play, per the NFL's Next Gen Stats, and have relied on the solid-but-uninspiring duo of Aaron Jones and Jordan Mason to lead its rushing attack this season.

Suffice it to say a three-down threat like Taylor would be a major upgrade for Minnesota's offense. His presence would allow Kevin O'Connell to shift the Vikings toward a ground-and-pound offensive mentality that would complement Brian Flores' aggressive, attacking-style defense well.

Taylor would also be a nice, long-term fit for the Vikings given his age (27) and the fact that he is under contract through the 2028 season. Jones is set to turn 32 in December while Mason, who is 27 like Taylor, will be a free agent after the season.

Seattle Seahawks

The Seahawks and Colts already swung one deal involving the aforementioned Nelson. Could they consider another?

Seattle's rushing offense hasn't been the same in 2026 after losing Kenneth Walker III to the Kansas City Chiefs in free agency. The Seahawks rank just 22nd in team rushing success rate, per the NFL's Next Gen Stats, with a mark of 38.8% and have seen their running backs average just 3.6 yards per carry collectively this season.

The Seahawks may be content to wait and see if the return of first-round rookie Jadarian Price and fourth-year veteran Zach Charbonnet can spark a resurgence in their running game. That said, the team's initial pursuit of Joe Mixon highlighted it isn't fully comfortable with what it has at running back, so perhaps John Schneider will be willing to pursue Taylor to improve Seattle's chances of repeating as Super Bowl champions.

More: 'Frustrated' Kenneth Walker III didn't shake hands with Seahawks after Chiefs' loss

Denver Broncos

The Broncos have started the 2026 NFL season with a 5-2 record despite a lackluster showing from their offense. Their running game has been particularly troublesome. They rank 30th in rush success rate this season, and primary ball-carriers J.K. Dobbins and RJ Harvey have combined to average 3.4 yards per carry this season.

Sean Payton may be content to see what fourth-round rookie Jonah Coleman can do in more of a lead-back role. He handled a team-high nine carries and turned them into 54 yards against the Arizona Cardinals in Week 7.

But if the Broncos want to add more of a sure thing at running back, Taylor would fit the bill. He would take a lot of pressure off Bo Nix and allow the Broncos to marry a more consistent, possession-oriented offense with the team's explosive defense.

New York Giants

The Giants' running game broke out in Week 7 against the Houston Texans, as Cam Skattebo responded to his benching by racking up 124 yards and a touchdown on 17 carries.

Will Skattebo's breakout be enough to earn John Harbaugh's trust long-term? Maybe, but given the success Harbaugh enjoyed with Derrick Henry in Baltimore, he can't be ruled out from pursuing a player like Taylor, especially with the Giants having the inside track toward winning the NFC East.

Taylor and Skattebo would form a fearsome one-two punch at running back and allow J.J. McCarthy to operate in the game manager role for which he is best suited. That could help the Giants make a playoff push while also positioning them to properly support Jaxson Dart in 2027 when the 2025 first-round pick returns from a season-ending knee injury.

More: 7 NFL teams that should be buyers at 2026 trade deadline, including Chiefs

Washington Commanders

At 1-4-1, the Commanders may not look like a big-time buyer ahead of the 2026 NFL trade deadline. Still, they could kick the tires on Taylor given their dual need for a top-tier starting running back and for playmaking support surrounding Jayden Daniels.

Pairing Daniels and Taylor together for at least a couple of seasons should be appealing for the Commanders. They could craft their offensive identity around Taylor's three-down abilities and Daniels' mobility, and adding a three-down back would mitigate the effects of losing Terry McLaurin to a torn patellar tendon.

It's also worth noting Commanders coach Dan Quinn and general manager Adam Peters are on relatively hot seats and need to start stringing some wins together to have a chance at retaining their jobs beyond this season. Adding Taylor would help them do that while also providing the team with a needed, long-term upgrade at running back.

Green Bay Packers

OK, the Packers probably won't pursue Taylor now that Josh Jacobs is back from the commissioner's exempt list. However, if Green Bay is worried about Jacobs facing an additional suspension for his offseason arrest, it could acquire an insurance option at the running back position.

Taylor would represent the high-end range for the Packers to consider, and it's fun to imagine how their offense would look with two big-time threats at the running back position. But more likely, the Packers will look to acquire a lower-priced veteran – like Tyjae Spears or Kimani Vidal – who can serve as an upgrade over MarShawn Lloyd (2.6 yards per carry) behind Jacobs.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Colts change course on Jonathan Taylor trade, insider says. What to know

item.title: Colts reportedly open to trading RB Jonathan Taylor before Nov. 10 deadline
item.description: Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner were already moved this week. Could Taylor be the next to go?
item.content:encoded:
The Indianapolis Colts are open to trading running back Jonathan Taylor, according to ESPN's Adam Schefter and NFL Network's Ian Rapoport.

After a week where the 2-5 Colts began a fire sale by moving guard Quenton Nelson and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner, while also being told by wide receiver Josh Downs that he would like to be traded, Taylor could be the biggest transaction made by interim general manager Ed Dodds ahead of the Nov. 10 trade deadline.

Taylor said this week that he met with Colts owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon to talk about his future with the team. While the team originally wanted to keep the 27-year-old running back as part of its rebuild, that sentiment has apparently changed, especially knowing the type of return the three-time Pro Bowler could deliver.

Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Taylor confirmed that he did not request a trade, but understood that he isn't in control of the situation.

"I'm proud to wear the horseshoe, proud to be here. Similar to Quenton [Nelson] and [DeForest Buckner], they were proud to wear the horseshoe, they were proud to be here," Taylor said. "But obviously, circumstances may cause otherwise. Hopefully that day may not come, but I can't control that."

There are already a number of suitors interested in acquiring Taylor. According to Schefter and Rapoport, the Denver Broncos, Green Bay Packers, Minnesota Vikings, New York Giants and Seattle Seahawks are among the teams who have inquired.

The Colts would reportedly be looking for a futures-heavy return in a trade, much like the four draft picks that the Carolina Panthers acquired in 2022 when they moved running back Christian McCaffrey to the San Francisco 49ers.

By trading Nelson and Buckner, the Colts gained third- and fourth-round draft picks in 2027 and a fifth-rounder in 2028. They currently do not own a 2027 first-rounder as that went to the New York Jets in the Sauce Gardner trade.

Taylor signed a two-year, $44 millon extension in August with $39 million in guaranteed money. The extension runs through the 2028 season with his salary cap hit at $16.2 million this season, $21 million in 2027 and just under $23 million in 2028, according to Over the Cap.

There is no word if the Colts will sit Taylor out for their Week 8 game against the Jacksonville Jaguars for asset protection. Despite his trade request, Downs will play on Sunday after head coach Shane Steichen told him, "You've got to show up and we gotta go play a game on Sunday."

Taylor has rushed for at least 1,100 yards in four of his six NFL seasons and has just under 600 yards through seven games this season.
