item.title: Raiders Mailbag: Should Las Vegas sell Maxx Crosby, Kolton Miller, other players ahead of NFL trade deadline?
item.description: Returning Raider Nation’s questions for the week
item.content:encoded:
The Las Vegas Raiders have a chance to end their four-game losing streak against the New York Jets in Week 8. But we’re also less than two weeks away from the NFL Trade Deadline (Tuesday, Nov. 10 at 1:00 p.m. PST), which is the primary focus of this week’s mailbag. Let’s get to it!

Q: Would be interesting to hear your take on trading Maxx Crosby, Jackson Powers-Johnson, Kolton Miller, Isaiah Palo-Mao and Kirk Cousins? Seems like the right thing to do given the team’s realistic timeline.

A: I’ll start with the elephant in the room. I was a strong proponent of trading Crosby in the offseason and still think it would be in the Raiders’ best long-term interests to get multiple high-end draft picks for the 29-year-old. I think two first-rounders is probably out of the question now, but it doesn’t hurt that Jeffery Simmons — who is the same age and was in the same draft class as Crosby — just got dealt for two firsts and a fourth, with a fifth going back to Chicago. Also, Simmons is only under contract for one more year than Crosby is.

So, I think John Spytek could get at least a comparable return for the edge rusher, and I don’t know how Spytek could say ‘no’ to an offer like that after the team’s playoff hopes came crumbling down this month. It doesn’t seem like Crosby is going anywhere, though, with Adam Schefter saying on Monday that “he means so much to that franchise” while pouring cold water on the trade talk/rumors. But if I’m calling the shots, I’m pulling the trigger if I can get at least a first- and a second-round pick for Crosby.

I touched on this last week; it feels like Powers-Johnson’s days in Las Vegas are numbered after getting benched. I don’t know if that happens ahead of the trade deadline, but barring a material change, I think JPJ will be shopped in the offseason. I liken it to Tyree Wilson from this past offseason, where a fresh start might be best for both sides, and don’t expect much more than a fifth-rounder in return.

I’m all the way out on trading Miller ahead of the deadline. I know he has regressed, but if the plan is to have Fernando Mendoza play at any point this year, I’m not trusting Charles Grant to protect Mendoza’s blindside. Grant has barely seen the field, and at least the coaching staff knows what it can get from Miller, who has been a good pass protector in the past and is still solid right now.

Could Grant be the long-term solution at left tackle? Sure, but turning the reins over to him now would be a massive risk, especially with a rookie quarterback/the future of the franchise. In the offseason, I could be convinced that it’s worth it to trade Miller because then the coaching staff has several months to get Grant ready and can bring in a veteran insurance policy in free agency. But midseason, trading Miller would be a bad idea, in my opinion.

If there’s an offer, Pola-Mao would be easy to part with since he’s just a backup and special teamer right now. I just don’t know if there’s much of a market for that, barring an injury over the next two weekends. If IPM gets dealt, don’t expect much more than a sixth- for seventh-round pick swap or just a seventh-rounder. Also, he’s an impending free agent, so I could see Pola-Mao getting waived after the deadline to make room for Dalton Johnson on the game-day active roster.

I feel like I’m in the minority on this, but I would rather see the Raiders hold onto Cousins even if Mendoza is playing. Trust me, as a draft freak, I love the idea of getting more picks. However, I think it reduces part of the rationale for having Cousins be Mendoza’s mentor if the former gets shipped away when the latter takes over.

I know that has to happen at some point, but I think it’s valuable for the rookie to have a peer as a sounding board when things go wrong during his first handful of starts. Especially since Cousins has seen it all in the NFL, and those two have been forming a big brother-little brother type of relationship over the last six months.

A: Well, as someone who watches and breaks down the Raiders’ defense every week, the past month was already pretty unwatchable, LOL! But to your point, if Crosby does get traded, that creates a need for an edge and adds to the already rather long list of needs. That’s why I wouldn’t make that trade for just one first-round pick, and the return would have to include multiple Top 100 selections.

The plan for a Crosby-less defense in Vegas would hinge on Keyron Crawford bouncing back from injury and at least proving to be a quality second edge defender since Malcolm Koonce is on a one-year contract and Kwity Paye is trending toward being a bust/role player. Then, that’s where the two picks come in because one can be used to find Crosby’s replacement or the second edge if Crawford fills that role, and the second pick fills a different need like defensive tackle.

Obviously, there are a lot of variables that can go wrong in there. But the defense has given up over 35 points per game over the last four weeks with Crosby on it. Several positions need to be addressed in the offseason, and he’ll be 30 in August. So, would you rather have a very good but aging player, or two chances to improve the team for the long haul?

It’s a matter of preference, and there’s a good amount of risk involved in either scenario. But, again, I’d take my chances if the right offer comes across the desk.

Q: Is it time to have a realistic discussion on Spytek?

A: I got a lot of questions about Spytek this week, with several people asking if (or outright saying) he should get fired. I get it, the Raiders need to get a lot more return on their offseason investments. There’s no denying that, and Spytek’s Day 2 picks have produced little to nothing. Darien Porter is the best one so far, and Porter hasn’t been able to hold down a starting spot.

But part of the reason why the organization can’t get out of the downward spiral that it’s been in over the last two decades is that there has been no stability when it comes to the head coach and general manager. Granted, the Raiders didn’t have a true GM until Reggie McKenzie was hired in 2012, but it’s not like Mark Davis has been patient with his decision-makers.

To be fair, McKenzie got seven years. But even he had a few dud offseasons before putting together the 2016 roster, which has been the franchise’s best team since making the Super Bowl over 20 years ago. To put it in perspective, the Raiders were 10-37 during McKenzie’s first three years. Then, he had a great draft in 2014 (Khalil Mack, Derek Carr and Gabe Jackson), signed some quality free agents (Rodney Hudson, Kelechi Osemele and Michael Crabtree), and hit on his 2015 first-round pick (Amari Cooper) to put together a quality roster.

The problem was that 2017 was a major disappointment, so Davis fired Jack Del Rio and hired Jon Gruden, which essentially stripped any power away from McKenzie and led to his firing a year later. In stepped Mike Mayock for three seasons until Gruden’s email scandal led to another leadership turnover, where Davis brought in the Josh McDaniels-Dave Ziegler duo for a season-and-a-half. That didn’t work out, so it was Tom Telesco’s turn for a year, only for Tom Brady to come in and hire Spytek.

At some point, the Raiders have to stick with a plan and ride it out, even if the road gets bumpy.

General managers — especially ones taking over bad teams/rosters, which is the majority of them — get hired because of the long-term plan they present to the owner, which typically is a three- to four-year vision. However, Davis hasn’t given a GM three seasons since Mayock, who was hired pre-COVID, and McKenzie is the only one of the five GMs Davis has hired to get four or more years!

Do I think it’s fair to say Spytek should face criticism and feel a lot of pressure right now? Absolutely. But this franchise needs stability, and firing a third general manager in five years would be a mistake. The other thing to consider is who is going to want the job if three people who previously held the position were given, at most, two years to turn it around. In my opinion, Davis, Brady or whoever is calling the shots have to give Spytek another offseason.

A: I agree with you. The offensive line has certainly been frustrating, especially since the rushing stats look about the same as last year. But the difference between the 2025 and 2026 lines is that last year’s was a total mess where several players were having bad games every week. Whereas this year, it’s one guy letting the whole group down more often than not.

Now, part of the problem is the letdown lineman changes every game. One week it’s Spencer Burford, the next it’s whoever is at right guard, then it’s Tyler Linderbaum or Kolton Miller’s turn. DJ Glaze is the only one who has been decently consistent. The other issue is that the offensive line is a position group where all five players have to execute to get results.

This is an extreme example, but if four out of five linemen get pancakes on one play and say one of the guards whiffs trying to block a defensive tackle, the run is probably going to be a TFL or a short gain despite 80 percent of the line doing their jobs at a high level.

All of this is to say I do think Vegas’ line has improved from last year; it couldn’t get much worse. They just have to be more consistent individually to improve as a group and start getting results.

A: Unless someone (preferably a couple of players) steps up and surprises us in the second half of the season, I don’t think much is going to change when it comes to the Raiders’ offseason needs. To be fair, it sounds like Trey Zuhn III is going to get a chance to start and prove himself, and I thought Tim Keenan had a decent game as a practice squad call up last week. But even if those two show promise down the stretch, the Raiders are still going to need another starting guard and an interior pass-rusher.

There’s still a lot of football to play, so I won’t completely close the door. However, all signs are pointing toward the trenches being a big point of emphasis in Las Vegas this spring.

A: At least one of those positions is going to have to get addressed in free agency, and I’d lean toward the two trench spots. I’ll be keeping my eyes on Moro Ojomo and Kobie Turner at defensive tackle, and Quenton Nelson (unless the Seahawks give him an extension, of course) and Kevin Dotson at guard.

Wide receiver could get tricky because the Raiders are going to have to pick in the top three to get Jeremiah Smith, and that still might not be enough because Smith is good enough to be the first wideout taken No. 1 overall since Keyshawn Johnson in 1996. Also, the rest of the draft class has been fairly disappointing, making it difficult to find a true “first-round talent”. However, Charlie Becker has maintained his value, and it would be intriguing to reunite him with Fernando Mendoza.

Ultimately, it’s going to depend on where the Raiders are drafting and how the rest of the College Football season plays out. So it’s a little early for this type of question. However, generally speaking, I think Vegas needs to prioritize the trenches in the offseason before addressing the skill positions.

That’s killing both sides of the ball more than the wide receivers or defensive backs are, and it is trending that there will be some decent Day 2 options in this year’s wideout class. It just doesn’t have as much top-end talent as many (including myself) thought there would be heading into the fall.

Q: Is Quay Walker actually just bad?

A: For some context, I’ve noted in winners and losers that opposing offenses have been targeting Walker in coverage and having a lot of success over the last few weeks, and I broke down what that looked like against the Rams on the Tape Don’t Lie review of the game.

Walker is playing well as a run defender, currently owning a career-high 71.4 run defense grade from Pro Football Focus that ranks 25th among linebackers this season. And he’s typically fine in man coverage, where he can lean on his natural gifts and doesn’t have to think as much.

However, the former first-round pick’s awareness/instincts in zone coverage are the primary reason why he hasn’t lived up to his draft potential, and that’s reared its head over the last few weeks. Also, he has a bad habit of not plastering to his man on scramble drills.

When the Raiders signed Walker in free agency, I was hopeful that he’d start to put it together in year five and that reuniting with Nakobe Dean would take enough off the former Packer’s plate since Dean wears the green dot and takes control of getting the defense set in Las Vegas. But that hasn’t made a difference, as Walker’s issues in Green Bay traveled with him to Vegas.

Now, he’s still only 26 years old, and we still have half a season left to play. So, there’s time for him to bounce back and improve down the line. However, it certainly isn’t comforting to see that a $13.5 million per year linebacker’s biggest weakness still exists and hasn’t gotten any better.

A: It’s kind of funny; typically, this question is the other way around, where running out of the shotgun isn’t as effective. But that’s just how backward the Raiders’ rushing attack is, where I’m sitting here saying: “Why not try it?” LOL! It can’t get much worse!

That being said, I think it would break every fiber in Klint Kubiak’s body to run out of the shotgun. It isn’t in his DNA, literally, since Gary Kubiak was a big under center coordinator/coach, too. Outside of draws, I feel like I’ve seen the Raiders run the ball from the gun like twice this year. I’m probably exaggerating there a bit, but the team does rank 21st in shotgun usage (including pass plays) according to Sumer Sports.

In other words, I’d be surprised to see it, but Kubiak might as well try to mix it up because what he’s currently trying isn’t working.

That’ll do it for this week’s mailbag. Thank you all for submitting questions and, as your weekly reminder, if you’d like to have your questions answered in a future column, tweet them at me, @MHolder95, email them to SBPQuestions1@gmail.com or look for our weekly call for questions on the site. The latter will continue to publish on Thursdays.

FOX is set to televise the 1:o5 p.m. PDT kickoff from SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, Ca. With the two organizations sharing the same stadium, it is the Rams that have been designated as the home team.

2026 has been a struggle for the o-6 Chargers, but coming in to the game off a bye week, they should be refreshed, healed up, and ready for a clean slate. The Bolts have struggled on offense, rating in the Bottom 3 of the NFL in total points scored (90), total yards (1723), yards per play (4.6), passing yards (1009), percentage of drives ending in a score (25.4), and have the highest percentage of drives ending in a turnover (19.7).

On the other hand, the Rams are towards the top of NFL stats in both offense and defense. Allowing opponents (mostly lesser) to hang around too long, self-inflicted wounds, and horrendous special teams play has them needing this win to get back to .500 and stay within reach of the six teams that are ahead or tied with them in the wild card race.

The injury bug has really embedded under the Rams skin and Week 8 is no different. L.A. has four starters with a questionable designation, center Coleman Shelton (hip). tight end Colby Parkinson (ribs), wide receiver Jordan Whittington (back), and cornerback Trent McDuffie (groin). item.title: Prove Them Wrong: An Open Letter to the Minnesota Vikings
item.description: If someone could deliver this to KO and company, I would greatly appreciate it.
item.content:encoded:
Dear Minnesota Vikings,

As you may be aware, you are the most disrespected 6-0 NFL team that I have seen in my lifetime. Despite the fact that you are 2-0 in divisional games and have a defense that is allowing the league’s fewest points per game at 12.3, people are still calling you frauds. Those voices have only grown louder over the past few weeks, and now there are comparisons between your starting quarterback and the one you let go to New York. The promises of Kevin O’Connell in locker room speeches saying that this offense is going to improve reverberate off of a concrete wall into thin air. Yes, Kyler Murray is protecting the football and not committing costly turnovers. He has also been inconsistent at times and has missed quite a few throws due to poor timing or inaccuracy.

We thought this year was going to be different. Heck, Max Brosmer was 1-1 last year in games where he produced almost zero (if not negative) offensive value. Meanwhile, this season’s offense has to scratch and claw for 60 minutes just to score ONE TOUCHDOWN! We are witnessing the same problems with stagnancy (which seems to be a prevalent theme in your offensive scheme, Kevin) every time we have possession of the football. Every drive feels like ten steps forward with two steps back, culminating in a 50-yard Will Reichard field goal. I don’t even want to watch when you have the ball in between the 40s, because I know you aren’t going to get anywhere near the endzone. For example, this past week, Myles Price set you up with immaculate field position, and what did you do with it? You ran the ball four times and failed to convert on fourth down, turning the ball over on downs. RIDICULOUS.

The lack of production on offense is why everybody and their mamas with a microphone and a camera are posting their very loud opinions on the internet. This week you play a divisional rival in the Detroit Lions. This is a chance to prove that your team is elite in all three phases and a true Super Bowl contender. You cannot rely on the defense to hold teams to fewer than 13 points every game. The silver lining is that I believe this defense CAN hold ANY team to 13 points or fewer, but still, you cannot rely on their dominance every week. The tension in my soul wants the confirmation that this offense can score 30+ points when called upon. Nothing would make me happier than for you to shut up all of these armchair analyst CLOWNS who think they know everything about football even though they probably haven’t watched one snap of a Minnesota Vikings game.

However, at the end of the day, I am a Minnesota Vikings fan. I know this is a franchise built upon the foundation of excellence on defense. I am also starting to understand why all of these talking heads are so low on you, the Minnesota Vikings. It’s because when they watch you play, they’re bored. They don’t care about history; they just want to be entertained. Nothing is less entertaining to faux media jabronis than elite defense and low-scoring games. Maybe it is a personal problem that has compelled me to write this letter. Why do I expose myself to these opinions on social media and the internet? Part of it is so I can write informed pieces about the narratives surrounding this Vikings team. The other reason is that it fuels my passion. I see the potential, and I know that if this offense can start executing, this is going to be an incredibly scary team. Please, just shut the critics up. Please, please, PLEASE!

I now want to speak directly to you, Kevin. You need to get it together. I believe in your ability as a head coach in the NFL; I really do! You have cultivated a winning culture with this franchise, and the results have shown in the regular season. As I am sure you are aware, you have failed to lead this team to a single playoff victory in your tenure at the helm. Your system failed a young quarterback before he failed you (in some eyes), and as a coach brought in for your offensive prowess, you have not delivered on the expectation of efficient and effective offenses. So, what is the deal? Are you calling the right plays and your players just aren’t delivering the results? Are you lacking more explosive playmakers? Are you making the wrong decisions in certain situations, leading to uninspiring results? Do you need to focus more on managing the game and let someone else call the plays? What is it? All I’m going to say is, whatever the issue(s), please fix it. Figure it out so we can all stop asking these questions.

To the offense: you need to be better. I’m looking directly at you, Will Fries. You’ve done a nice job cleaning up some of the penalties we were seeing in the first few weeks of the season, but that’s not enough. You need to start scoring some touchdowns. Just know, the whole world is laughing at you and sees you as the downfall of an otherwise dominant team. You frequently start with great field position only to squander it. You have possessed the ball more than any other offense in the NFL, yet you’re in the bottom 5 of points scored (probably lower if you’re only counting touchdowns). Things just aren’t adding up, and you better start materializing the vision of your head coach.

You very well know the strength of your team is the defense. Blake, Eric, Jalen, Caleb, Dominique, Dallas, Andrew, Josh, Byron, Isaiah, and Harrison, I see the work you are putting in. Your excellence is not going unnoticed. You are part of an excellent and potentially historic defensive unit. You wreak so much havoc and create so much chaos that opposing offenses don’t know what to do to attack you. Sure, you’ve given up a few big plays this year and some touchdowns. However, you make the adjustments to thwart any offensive game plan. We saw it against Green Bay, New Orleans, and Indianapolis. You let Green Bay score 22 first-half points and then shut them out in the second half. You let New Orleans march down the field on a long drive and score a touchdown in the first quarter, only to hold them to 6 points for the rest of the game. You allowed Jonathan Taylor to break a long touchdown run, only to turn Danny Dimes into Danny Schillings and dominate the rest of the way. You are not the problem here, and I pray you continue to do what you do. Take care of your bodies and stay healthy, because we need you.

I will leave you with these parting words. I believe in the 2026 Minnesota Vikings. I have high hopes and expectations for this team. You will be playing meaningful football in January and possibly February. You have the leadership, drive, and determination to bring Minnesota its first Lombardi trophy. You just have to not get in your own way. Believe in yourselves, believe in each other, believe in the Minnesota Vikings’ culture. You have thousands of fans rooting for you, and we will be here with you until the possibly bitter, but hopefully glorious, end. You have my support and the support of many others. I speak for many when I say I love this team and only want the best for you.

Until Next Skol.

item.title: Buccaneers vs. Falcons final injury report: Emeka Egbuka ruled out for Sunday’s game
item.description: The Tampa Bay Buccaneers released their final injury report Friday ahead of Sunday’s NFC South matchup against the Atlanta Falcons, with wide receiver Emeka Egbuka officially ruled out and two other players listed as questionable. Egbuka (foot) did not participate in Friday’s practice after being limited Wednesday and Thursday. The rookie receiver has cleared concussion […]
item.content:encoded:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers released their final injury report Friday ahead of Sunday’s NFC South matchup against the Atlanta Falcons, with wide receiver Emeka Egbuka officially ruled out and two other players listed as questionable.

Egbuka (foot) did not participate in Friday’s practice after being limited Wednesday and Thursday. The rookie receiver has cleared concussion protocol, but his lingering foot injury will keep him sidelined for a second consecutive game.

Offensive tackle Luke Goedeke (calf) returned to practice on a limited basis Friday after missing the previous two sessions. He is listed as questionable for Sunday, along with running back Kenny Gainwell (hip), who was a full participant after steadily improving throughout the week.

The Buccaneers did receive some encouraging news elsewhere on the injury report. Quarterback Baker Mayfield (right thumb) and safety Antoine Winfield Jr. (rib) were full participants throughout the week and carry no injury designations into Sunday’s matchup.

Outside linebacker Yaya Diaby and linebacker Josiah Trotter, who were both dealing with illnesses earlier in the week, also practiced fully Friday and are expected to be available.

Meanwhile, Atlanta will be without running back Brian Robinson, who was ruled out with a hamstring injury after missing all three practices this week.

The Falcons also have eight players listed as questionable, including defensive back Billy Bowman Jr. (hamstring), linebacker Divine Deablo (forearm), defensive end Samson Ebukam (hamstring), cornerback Avieon Terrell (illness), defensive end Charles Snowden (back) and wide receiver Olamide Zaccheaus (shoulder).

Wide receiver Beaux Collins (hip) and offensive tackle Cameron Williams (ankle) are also questionable despite being full participants in Friday’s practice.

Both teams will announce their inactive players approximately 90 minutes before kickoff Sunday.

The Buccaneers (2-5) host the Falcons (3-4) at Raymond James Stadium on Sunday, November 1. Kickoff is scheduled for 1:00 p.m. ET.

item.title: Seahawks Reacts Survey results: Fans confident Seattle comes out on top over Bears
item.description: However, opinions are split regarding the win margin for the Seahawks.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Each week we ask questions of the most plugged-in Seattle Seahawks fans and fans across the country.

Coming off a dominant 20-3 victory over the previously undefeated Kansas City Chiefs—where both the offense as well as the defense appeared to be near the top of their game, the Seattle Seahawks are within two games of taking over first place in the NFC West. With the division leader San Francisco 49ers on a bye week, they have a chance to inch one step closer. But, it won’t come easy when they host the high-powered Chicago Bears, who have won four of their last five games.

Despite another tough matchup, there remains a high level of confidence Seattle can deliver a second consecutive win.

While fans are seemingly certain the Seahawks will collect another primetime win (94% of votes), the margin of victory has conflicting opinions. In a tight poll, the majority believes Seattle will produce a convincing victory by a 9-16 point margin, with 46% of votes trending in that direction. However, 42% of voters think they’ll still come out on top, but by less than a possession.

In addition, six percent of participants view a Seahawks victory by two or more possessions, whereas five percent believe the Bears will haul out a close win and one percent pessimistically think Chicago will prevail by 9+ points.

Given the recent success of Chicago and quarterback Caleb Williams, a Seahawks victory by more than one possession appears to be wishful thinking, but it’d be foolish to rule it out after their defense—nicknamed the ‘Dark Side’ sacked Patrick Mahomes once, picked him off and forced a fumble while holding one of the NFL’s most prolific offenses to just three points last week. As an added bonus, they held superstar running back Kenneth Walker III to just 36 yards on the ground and spoiled his return to Seattle.

It’s also worth noting quarterback Sam Darnold had arguably his best game of the season and although it may not have looked that way on paper, his confidence, composure and ability to find open receivers was a noticeable step up compared to where it was just a week before against the Denver Broncos.

On top of the Seahawks issues running the ball, Chicago’s allowing the third least amount of rushing yards per game (87.6), meaning Darnold is poised to be heavily relied upon to deliver through the air. With wide receiver Rashid Shaheed’s (knee) status in question after he failed to participate in either of the team’s first two practices of the week, Seattle’s receiving core appears likely to be shorthanded on Monday night.

Luckily for Seattle’s signal caller, general manager John Schneider acquired eight-time Pro Bowler Quenton Nelson—one of the league’s best guards on Tuesday to significantly boost their offensive line, one who’s allowed 16 sacks through seven games. As for Nelson, he’s only allowed one quarterback hit this year.

While he’s a significant upgrade over Anthony Bradford, Nelson and the rest of Seattle’s offensive line will be faced with stopping an impactful defensive line who just added All-Pro tackle Jeffrey Simmons via a trade with the Tennessee Titans.

Although they’re set to receive an addition in the trenches, the Seahawks pass could be in trouble if Shaheed is ultimately ruled out. Chicago ranks third in offensive yards per game (390.7), with playmakers all over the field. Williams and emerging star wideout Luther Burden III have connected on all targets so far this season, and Rome Odunze as well as Colston Loveland also profile as dangerous receiving option. As for their ground attack, running back D’Andre Swift has been consistent, having totalled 476 yards and seven touchdowns.

He’ll likely command the backfield once again with fellow back Kyle Monangai (toe, thumb) having logged two consecutive missed practices to open the week.

Williams has also proven to be a rushing threat, but hasn’t eclipsed 20+ yards since returning from a hamstring injury that sidelined him from Weeks 2-6. Whether Mike Macdonald and Seattle’s defense can apply enough pressure to prevent the dual-threat quarterback from utlizing his legs will likely impact the momentum and possibly, the final outcome.

Regardless, they’re one of the best offenses in the league, and if the Seahawks is forced to play from behind, it would hurt having Shaheed sidelined and potentially running back Zach Charbonnet (knee) as well—who was downgraded to a limited participant at Friday’s practice.

Outside of Shaheed and Charbonnet, linebacker Uchenna Nwosu (ankle), offensive tackle Charles Cross (ankle), running back Velus Jones Jr. (hamstring), and offensive guard Anthony Bradford (knee) were all non-participants in Friday’s practice. Cross’ absence isn’t surprising considering he was diagnosed with a high ankle sprain on Monday and is expected to miss time but it appears Seattle could possibly be without additional reinforcements against Chicago. A staple on Macdonald’s defense, it’ll be worth monitoring whether Nwosu is assigned an injury designation on Sunday.

Linebacker Tyrice Knight (hip), quarterback Drew Lock (right elbow) and Byron Murphy II (back) practiced in a limited capacity on Friday, so it’ll be worth monitoring their status’ leading up to kickoff as well.

Considering the Bears have won both of their primetime matchups this season and the Seahawks are likely to be without numerous starters, a multi-possession victory for the home side appears unlikely—even though it generated 52% of votes. However, given the nature of Seattle’s win over Kansas City, it’d be a disservice to count them out in any capacity.

The Seahawks are currently 3-point favorites on FanDuel and with questions hovering over both teams, a narrow, one-possession victory appears to be the most plausible heading into the weekend—although Seattle’s injury designations will likely provide a clearer picture. By the way, confidence is high among the fanbase once again.

item.title: Broncos vs. Chiefs: 3 Players to Watch in Week 8
item.description: These three players need big performances for the Denver Broncos to defeat the Kansas City Chiefs.
item.content:encoded:
The Denver Broncos host the Kansas City Chiefs on Sunday. It’s a shot for Denver to earn their fourth straight victory. Even better, the Broncos can be the top team in the AFC West by beating the Chiefs. In order to make that happen, these three players will have to perform at a high level.

Bo Nix — Quarterback

One good performance can be a catalyst and confidence boost for players hoping to get things going in the right direction. It wasn’t perfect by any means, but quarterback Bo Nix’s outing versus the Arizona Cardinals had quite a few bright spots. It also answered a few lingering questions Broncos Country and many analysts.

The concerns on Nix’s ability to run should be put to bed after his transcendent 62-yard touchdown gallop. What I liked even more was his aggressiveness and willingness to throw the ball down the field. Nix was able to make some tight down the field throws against Cover 2 shells and delivered a handful of impressive throws on middle of the field concepts. Those splash plays were hard to come by in prior games.

Steve Spagnuolo’s defense has been one of the best in the NFL to start the season. Even though their top two corners from last season are playing elsewhere, their passing defense has still been stellar. They’ve done a good job limiting explosive plays and keeping most top targets from doing much damage through the air.

Nix and the Broncos’ aerial attack had just 115 passing yards in Week 1. That won’t be good enough to earn a victory on Sunday, so improvement will be necessary. Keep in mind, the Chiefs have forced ten turnovers in six games, with two in four contests—including two against the Broncos on Monday Night Football. Nix will need to find a way to be effective and not turn the ball over.

Alex Singleton — Linebacker

Alex Singleton’s Week 1 outing against the Chiefs was a big disappointment. Though it’s safe to say Singleton has really turned things around since then. In fact, this last three game stretch might be the best Broncos Country has seen from Singleton donning orange and blue.

Against the Cardinals, Singleton was a heat-seeking missile. He notched an incredible 19 tackles and came away with several quarterback pressures and a key sack. That earned him AFC Defensive Player of the Week honors.

Running back Kenneth Walker has been an explosive playmaker for the Chiefs. He is the engine that makes their offense go and certainly one of the NFL’s premier offensive weapons. Everyone knows limiting his impact is a big key to the game. Walker was absolutely dominant in Kansas City’s Week 1 pummeling of the Broncos.

However, the Seattle Seahawks found a way to shut last year’s Super Bowl MVP in their Week 7 win over the Chiefs. He can be stopped. This time around, I’m optimistic Singleton and the Broncos’ defense will execute far better this time around and slow down Kansas City’s rushing attack.

Jonah Coleman — Running Back

As the Broncos gear up for the second half stretch of the season, establishing a formidable rushing attack will be critical. Last week against the Cardinals, the Broncos put together their best run game performance of the season. Rookie running back Jonah Coleman was a big part of that and was productive with his touches.

After the game, Head Coach Sean Payton vowed to get Coleman more touches moving forward. That seems like a good bet with RJ Harvey’s status versus the Chiefs in doubt. I expect this to be a tough and gritty matchup with both teams trying to dictate the pace of the game on the ground.

Denver’s offense has struggled to convert third downs all season long. There is no simple fix to that issue. However, I believe getting quality yards on early downs would certainly help. They have been in far too many third-and-long situations.

Head Coach Sean Payton has been insistent trying to rectify the Broncos’ first down passing woes since he took over playcalling duties. This Sunday, I’d like to see a little more emphasis running consistently on first down—especially early on in games.

Coleman has performed well that regard in limited playing time. He is averaging 4.7 yards per carry on first downs. He’s also more effective than J.K. Dobbins on second down rushes. I’d like to see Denver showcase the rookie running back against the Chiefs. It’s a big opportunity for him to show he should be leading the Broncos’ rushing group moving forward.

item.title: Giants' John Harbaugh called Titans owner directly in attempt to trade for All-Pro DT Jeffery Simmons
item.description: The Giants are in the market for DT help ahead of the NFL trade deadline, and according to a recent report, head coach John Harbaugh has been active in their pursuit.
item.content:encoded:
The Giants are in the market for DT help ahead of the NFL trade deadline, and according to Jonathan Jones of the Athletic, head coach John Harbaugh has gotten active in their pursuit. 

Jones notes that Harbaugh called Titans owner Amy Adams Strunk directly in an attempt to trade for star pass rusher Jeffrey Simmons in a bit of an unorthodox move during NFL trade discussions.  

GM Joe Schoen had previously spoken with Tennessee's front office as well, but at the time, they told him and other interested clubs they weren't looking to move on from Simmons. 

Harbaugh is said to have gotten the same message from Strunk during their conversation, but after a 1-6 start to the season, the Titans ended up dealing Simmons to the Bears for a pair of first-round picks. 

Simmons certainly would've provided a significant boost for the middle of Big Blue's defense. 

The 29-year-old is coming off his first All-Pro season in which he recorded a career-high 11.0 sacks. 

He's racked up four more sacks through the first seven games this year, to go along with total 38 tackles (six for a loss) and a team-leading four passes defended. 

According to Jones, the Giants remain active in their pursuit of DT and RB help ahead of the deadline.

item.title: Colts willing to trade RB Jonathan Taylor, per report
item.description: The Indianapolis Colts are believed to be ready to trade Jonathan Taylor, and the NY Giants could be potential trade partners
item.content:encoded:
The Indianapolis Colts are now willing to trade star running back Jonathan Taylor, per a report from Adam Schefter of ESPN.

Schefter adds in his report that the New York Giants are among the teams thought to have at least “some level of interest” in trading for Taylor. Schefter also lists the Seattle Seahawks, Denver Broncos, Minnesota Vikings, Green Bay Packers as teams believed to be interested in trading for Taylor.

It’s no secret that while new Giants head coach John Harbaugh likes the trio of Cam Skattebo, Tyrone Tracy, and Devin Singletary, he has coveted a “bellcow” running back.

The Giants reportedly pursued Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker III in free agency and it was likewise reported that star Notre Dame running back Jeremiyah Love was tied with Arvell Reese at the top of their board. It was widely believed that the Giants would have drafted Love at fifth overall if he was still available.

One of the issues with the Giants’ backfield is that while they lack an explosive option out of the backfield, and Taylor has been one of the NFL’s most explosive runners. Last year he was tied for sixth in the NFL with 16 designed runs of 15+ yards, and was third in “breakaway” runs. He also led the NFL with 18 rushing touchdowns to just two (2) fumbles last year.

Our own Ed Valentine wrote earlier this week that the Giants should capitalize on their opportunity to win the NFC East this year and go all-in on the 27-year old Taylor.

After a report that head coach John Harbaugh personally called Tennessee Titans ownership in an effort to get defensive tackle Jeffrey Simmons, who landed with the Chicago Bears, you can expect the Giants to be aggressive in pursuit of Taylor.

The move would likely cost significant draft capital, possibly a first round pick to replace the one the Colts traded to the New York Jets. That’s real consideration oncern in a 2027 draft class that’s shaping up to be very talented and deep at a number of positions of need for the Giants. Acquiring Taylor would also require significant cap space and financial maneuvering.

However, the argument is that Taylor is among the very best runners in the NFL and could complete a true “three headed monster” with wide receiver Malik Nabers and tight end Isaiah Likely.

And frankly, if Taylor becomes the apple of Harbaugh’s eye, it becomes Joe Schoen’s job to do everything in his power to acquire the running back.

So what do you think Giants’ fans? Do you think the Giants are serious contenders for Taylor? And should they be?

item.title: Report: John Harbaugh called Amy Adams Strunk directly in an effort to land Jeffery Simmons
item.description: Harbaugh's unconventional move failed to prevent Bears from doing deal with Titans.
item.content:encoded:
The trade that sent defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons from the Titans to the Bears has an interesting — and unusual — postscript.

Jonathan Jones of The Athletic reports that Giants coach John Harbaugh directly called Titans owner Amy Adams Strunk in an effort to get Simmons to New York.

The call reportedly came after Giants G.M. Joe Schoen had contacted Titans G.M. Mike Borgonzi about Simmons, only to be told that the Titans weren't trading him.

As Jones notes, another G.M. who learned about the effort said it "violates a code" among football's decision-makers. One source in a key football position with one of the NFL's teams dubbed the effort "shameful."

Despite Borgonzi's claim from Thursday that the Titans weren't looking to trade Simmons until the Bears called on Wednesday night, Jones reports that the Titans' "braintrust" had a meeting on Tuesday during which they decided to start listening to offers for Simmons.

It's unclear whether Harbaugh made the call to Adams before or after Bears G.M. Ryan Poles offered a package that included a pair of first-round picks. We're told the Giants were willing to offer more than what the Bears ultimately sent to the Titans. (Of course, that's easy to say at this point.)

The entire situation underscores the value of pre-existing relationships when it comes to getting deals done. It was a point we discussed on Friday's PFT Live. In 2021, the trade that sent quarterback Matthew Stafford from the Lions to the Rams had a distinct "inside job" feel to it, given that Lions G.M. Brad Holmes had recently been hired from the Rams.

Other teams that would have been interested in attempting to acquire Stafford were surprised to learn that he had been quietly and quickly dealt to the Rams, who were able to tuck quarterback Jared Goff into the deal — and to discreetly attach extra compensation to get the Lions to take on a contract that, after only two seasons, the Rams had come to regret. The outcome prompted former Commanders G.M. Martin Mayhew to call every team in the league the following offseason to inquire as to whether their starting quarterback may be available in trade.

The ultimate question, when trades like this happen, is whether the relationship angle results in the team that gives up a key player getting as much as it could. If the Giants would have indeed offered more, shouldn't the Titans have fully explored that avenue? Ultimately, the longstanding relationship between Poles and Borgonzi may have superseded the effort to get as much as possible for Simmons.

item.title: Myles Garrett, Micah Parsons injury updates could impact Browns NFL draft stock
item.description: Injury updates on Myles Garrett, Micah Parsons could have a big impact on the Cleveland Browns 2027 NFL draft
item.content:encoded:
For two teams that do not play against each other this season, the Cleveland Browns and Los Angeles Rams are uniquely linked this season because of the Myles Garrett trade. While the Rams bounced back in Week 7, injuries continue to be a big story for a team that was expected to be the Super Bowl favorite and started the year with four losses already.

It all started with Los Angeles’ loss in Week 1, in Australia, which was followed by Garrett having surgery and going on injured reserve. In early October, the Rams still didn’t have a timeline for when Garrett would return, and he is now set to miss Week 8, with uncertainty about when he could return to practice.

Once Los Angeles opens Garrett’s return-to-practice timeline, it still could be multiple weeks before he’s back on the field. With the NFL trade deadline two game weeks away, the Rams could be in a difficult position after Week 10.

On top of that, with or without Garrett, LA looks like they will be facing fellow star pass rusher Micah Parsons on Thanksgiving Eve against the Green Bay Packers:

Parsons had ACL surgery after being injured last year, but has taken longer to return to the field than others who had a similar injury and timeframe.

The NFL is a week-to-week league, so assuming anything about what will happen in Week 12 of the season is a bit foolhardy. By then, Garrett could have returned and helped the Rams turn their season all the way around, while the Packers could have hit a slump without their top pass rusher.

For now, Browns fans will continue to keep one eye on anything and everything related to the Rams, while looking for their team to make a big push to the NFL playoffs.

item.title: ‘Kudos and Wet Willies’, plus bye week thoughts on every Giants defensive player
item.description: Reviewing the Giants’ defense at the bye week — who has played well, and who needs to step up.
item.content:encoded:
The New York Giants defense under coordinator Dennard Wilson has become an aggressive unit that is playing well despite the loss of Brian Burns, questions on the defensive line, and churn in the secondary due to injuries. Let’s go position-by-position with Kudos, Wet Willies, and thoughts on every player.

Defensive line

D.J. Reader — Dexter Lawrence is an elite player who has returned to form this season with the Cincinnati Bengals. It isn’t worth crying over spilt milk, though. Reader has been everything the Giants could have hoped for in a replacement. Maybe more.

Pro Football Focus, in fact, ranks Reader as the best defensive tackle in football so far this season with an elite 90.4 grades. Lawrence (87.6) is No. 2).

Want to see a major difference in grading systems? Pro Football and Sports Network, which puts much more weight on pass rush, has Reader as its 53rd-ranked defensive tackle, with Lawrence at No. 2.

Regardless of all of the number gobbledygook (now that’s a cool Halloween word), Reader has been outstanding for the Giants. They just need to get him some help.

Grade: Kudos

Shelby Harris — The fact that Harris is the Giants’ second-best defensive lineman tells you why the position is an issue, and a priority for the team to address before the Nov. 10 NFL trade deadline. The 35-year-old, in his 13th NFL season, is not the player he once was.

Statistical sites, in fact, tell us that Harris is clearly having what is by far the worst season of his career.

Pro Football Focus tells us Harris is No. 102 of 126 qualifying defensive tackles, and that his 49.2 grade is the first would be the first time in his career he has graded below 60.0.

Pro Football and Sports Network shows a similar degradation in Harris’ play.

Harris is still playing a ton of snaps (238 thus far, 54%), and doing what he can. At this point in his career, though, the Giants appear to be asking too much of him.

Grade: Kwillie

Darius Alexander — One reason the Giants are asking so much of the aging Harris is that Alexander, a 2025 third-round pick, has not given them enough. PFSN ranks Alexander 119th among 121 qualifying defensive tcles this season, and PFF ranks him No. 102 of 147 qualifiers in their grading system.

Alexander’s talent and athleticism tell you he should be much more than he has been.

Grade: Wet Willie

Bobby Jamison-Travis — The rookie sixth-round pick did not see action until Week 6 against the New Orleans Saints. He played well against the run vs. the Houston Texans in Week 7, giving reason to hope he can contribute, but 42 total defensive snaps is not enough to give a legitimate grade.

Grade: Incomplete

C.J. Okoye — The Giants acquired the 6-foot-6, 365-pound 24-year-old from the Baltimore Ravens, where he had played for John Harbaugh, for the low price of a 2028 seventh-round pick. They hoped Okoye would take a step forward in his development and become a solid rotational run defender. It hasn’t happened, and Okoye has played just 87 defensive snaps (14.5 per game) across six games. A man as big and strong as Okoye shouldn’t be pushed out of a hole by blockers as easily and as often as Okoye is.

Grade: Wet Willie

Chauncey Golston — The veteran defensive end had earned a big role on defense before a neck injury short-circuited his season.

Grade: Incomplete

Edge defender

Abdul Carter — The No. 3 overall pick in the 2025 NFL Draft has spent the season reminding everyone why the Giants drafted him so high a year ago. His sack numbers (2.0) just don’t yet reflect how good the 23-year-old has actually been.

Carter has been a nightmare for opposing blockers this season, and is one one three qualifying edge defenders with elite Pro Football Focus grades of 90.0 or higher. With a 90.3 mark, he joins Will Anderson (90.8) and Aidan Hutchinson (92.2). PFSN penalizes him for the lack of sacks, ranking him a ridiculousy low No. 58 among 122 qualifiers.

Carter had a rocky rookie season, marked by maturity issues. This season, he has stepped up as both a player and as a vocal locker room leader.

Grade: Kudos

Kayvon Thibodeaux — The No. 5 pick in the 2022 NFL Draft is always a lightning rod for disagreement when it comes to trying to assess his play.

The pure numbers would tell you that Thibodeaux, starting after Brian Burns’ unfortunate season-ending injury, has been terrible and the Giants should either trade him before the upcoming deadline or happily let him walk in free agency at season’s end. He is 12th on the team in tackles (15), doesn’t have a tackle for loss or a sack, and has just one quarterback hit.

But, there are other more advanced and less visible to the naked eye measures that tell you there are plenty of ways in which Thibodeaux has been quietly effective.

Two things can be true at the same time, and in this case probably are. Thibodeaux is a good player, and if he were a third-round pick he would probably be looked at as a fantastic find at that point in the draft. Quietly effective, though, is not what you are hoping for from a No. 5 overall pick.

Grade: Kwillie

Brian Burns — I feel terrible for Burns. He is a pro’s pro, a nice guy, and a locker room leader who approaches and plays the game the right way. In eight NFL seasons, though, Burns has never had the good fortune of playing for a team that has made the playoffs. This Giants team has the chance to do that, and his season-ending knee injury means Burns won’t have a chance to help make that happen.

Grade: Incomplete

Trace Ford — The second-year former undrafted free agent gets credit for perseverance. The Giants cut him in 2025, and he spent part of the season on the team’s practice squad. They cut him again this year, and he again landed on the practice squad. Burns’ injury opened an opportunity for him to be a game-day elevation, and he parlayed that into a spot on the 53-man roster.

Ford has shown some potential with 10 tackles and three hurries over four games and 70 defensive snaps.

Grade: Kudos

Inside linebacker

Arvell Reese — I don’t care how good David Bailey, Jeremiyah Love, or Carnell Tate turn out to be, how did the New York Jets, Arizona Cardinals, and Tennessee Titans let this guy fall to the Giants with the fifth pick in the 2026 NFL Draft?

“Man, how good has he been? He’s been awesome. He’s been phenomenal since the day he got here,” GM Joe Schoen said during his bye week press conference. “And that’s probably why Coach and I, even in that [draft] video, we were shocked he was there. So, he’s just a quiet kid that goes about his business and he’s all ball all the time.

“That play he made the other day where he should have had the sack on (Houston Texans quarterback) C.J. (Stroud) and then turns around and hauls tail all the way down the field and puts the guy flat on his back while punching for the ball. I mean, you don’t see many people with his size that can move like that. And then just, that’s internal. That’s just want to. To go towards the quarterback and then turn and run, you can’t coach that. You either got that or you don’t. And his effort and the way he plays and flies around, I mean, you see him on film, he’s moving at a different speed than everybody else. And he’s just so big and fast and violent. So, we’re ecstatic to have him. We’re excited to see what the future holds.”

Reese is probably already the Giants’ best defensive player. ESPN recently ranked Reese and Sonny Styles as co-No. 1s in a post naming the top 10 rookies. ESPN’s Jordan Reid wrote:

Reese’s physicality and speed have shown up right away at the NFL level. He is comfortable attacking downhill as a run defender, and his consistency in coverage has been excellent. His four pass breakups are tied for the second most among all linebackers in 2026.

Reese is the ultimate playmaker who can not only be used on the second level but is also equally as effective as a blitzer. He has 10 pass-rush wins and two pass breakups on 93 blitz attempts this season. Reese is a key building block for the Giants’ defense alongside 2025 first-round pick Abdul Carter.

Grade: Kudos … If there was a higher grade, a ‘super Kudos’, I’d give it to Reese.

Tremaine Edmunds — Edmunds was the Giants’ leading tackler and defensive signal-caller before being lost for the season. His size and athleticism next to Reese will be missed, even though Micah McFadden is a quality player.

Grade: Incomplete

Micah McFadden — A Week 1 foot injury cost McFadden a chance at a big free agent contract last offseason. He re-signed a one-year “prove it” deal with the Giants. Only, with Reese and Edmunds in front of him, McFadden was stuck playing special teams and waiting for a chance.

He did not complain. With Edmunds out for the season, McFadden’s chance is here now. There are flaws in his game, but if he continues to play like he did Sunday against the Houston Texans, McFadden should find a nice free agent payday waiting for him somewhere this offseason.

Grade: Kudos … Maybe one full game at linebacker should make this an incomplete, but McFadden’s attitude and readiness to play vs. the Texans and be the defensive signal-caller deserves recognition.

Malik Harrison — A seven-year veteran, Harrison is a key special teams player for the Giants. Defensively, though, he has played just four snaps.

Grade: Incomplete

Zaire Barnes — Like Harrison, Barnes is a key special teams player who does not have a defensive role. He has played just three defensive snaps.

Grade: Incomplete

Jack Kelly — A sixth-round pick, Kelly showed promise during training camp. He has yet to play a defensive snap this season, with his role confined strictly to special teams.

Grade: Incomplete

Cornerback

Deonte Banks — Banks has gone from a player with his future in question after back-to-back rough seasons, to one playing the way the Giants hoped he would when they traded up to make him a first-round pick in 2023. Against Nico Collins last Sunday, Banks looked like a No. 1 cornerback.

Is there any doubt the Giants need to give Banks a contract extension.

Here is some of his work this season:

Banks did this on the final play of a game against the Arizona Cardinals to secure a victory:

Banks has accepted coaching, is playing in an aggressive scheme that allows him to be an athlete, has taken ownership of a couple of plays he did not make, and is having fun.

Grade: Kudos

Greg Newsome — It was fair to wonder which version of Newsome the Giants would get this season. Would they get the former first-round pick of the Cleveland Browns who played really well in his first couple of seasons, or the guy who played like an untrustworthy journeyman the last couple of years. They have gotten the former.

Grade: Kudos

Dru Phillips — Phillips is an aggressive run defender and overall good player who has a nasty habit of getting grabby in coverage. Phillips has five penalties this second, second-most among defensive backs to Kamari Lassiter of the Houston Texans, who has 6.

Grade: Kwillie

Colton Hood — The Giants believe that the rookie second-round pick will eventually develop into a reliable starting-caliber cornerback. He has played 125 snaps, and his 138.5 passer rating against, per Pro Football Reference, shows that he isn’t there yet.

Grade: Kwillie

Paulson Adebo — Adebo did not play well in a Week 1 10-snap cameo, then went on IR with a knee injury. He returned in Week 7 and played well against the Texans, playing every snap in place of the injured Newsome.

Grade: Incomplete

Nic Jones — He is mostly a special teams player, with only 36 defensive snaps played so far this season. My impression has always been that he could be more, but he hasn’t had the chance.

Grade: Incomplete

Nikko Reed — Does anyone even remember when the Giants signed Reed off the Los Angeles Chargers practice squad in mid-September? He has yet to play a defensive snap.

Grade: Incomplete

Safety

Jevon Holland — Holland won the Giants Week 3 game against Tennessee with an end zone interception in the closing seconds. He already has a career-high three interceptions after getting just six over his first five NFL seasons. He has also forced two fumbles.

Grade: Kudos

Tyler Nubin — Nubin’s issues are the same as they have always been. When he takes a bad angle in the open field, his athleticism betrays him and tackles that should be made turn into big plays. The ball-hawking ability he showed in college has never translated to the NFL.

Nubin missed Week 6 with a neck injury and played only one emergency snap in Week 7. When the Giants return from their bye, it will be interesting to see if Jason Pinnock has taken his starting job. In the meritocracy in which the Giants are operating, that would not be a surprise.

Grade: Kwillie

Jason Pinnock — Pinnock was really good for the Giants in Wink Martindale’s aggressive defense in 2023.

Grade: Kudos

Ar’Darius Washington — Washington is a useful veteran player who can fill a number of roles in the secondary. He has not, though, been able to surpass Tyler Nubin or Jason Pinnock on the depth chart.

Grade: Kwillie

Elijah Campbell — Campbell is a career special teams player. He has not played a single defensive snap, while logging 158 on special teams. He only played 16 defensive snaps for the Miami Dolphins last season.

Grade: Incomplete

item.title: Vikings vs. Lions preview: 5 small weaknesses in Minnesota’s defense
item.description: A data-driven preview of Vikings at Lions, focusing on key stats and matchups.
item.content:encoded:
Riding a two-game winning streak, the Detroit Lions have a massive home-field opportunity to knock the NFL’s last remaining undefeated team off its warship throne, move within striking distance of first place in the NFC North, and exact revenge for last year’s two defeats to the Vikings, both highly uncharacteristic of the team’s identity under Dan Campbell. Prior to last season, Campbell had won five straight games against Kevin O’Connell, including four in a row with Brian Flores as defensive coordinator.

The Lions’ quest to regain the throne of the North will ride on the shoulders of their All-Pro-caliber backfield duo of Jared Goff and Jahmyr Gibbs, and an offense facing a Vikings defense under Flores that is off to a historically lethal start, pillaging opponents on its way to a 6-0 record (11 wins straight dating back to last season).

With the stakes incredibly high for Halloween weekend, this week’s preview dives into the cranium of Detroit’s Megamind, Drew Petzing, as he squares off against not just Flores but his former quarterback, Kyler Murray. We’ll examine how the Lions’ offense can keep the monsters from underneath their bed.

Note: Unless otherwise indicated, all statistics are sourced from NFL Pro, FTN Fantasy, Pro Football Reference, SumerSports, or Pro Football Focus.

The Trojan Norse

The Minnesota Vikings’ pass defense, with its 70.0%+ blitz rate, has been nightmare fuel for opposing quarterbacks. They lead the league in EPA/dropback allowed (-0.323), success rate allowed (38.2%), sack rate (10.1%), and pressure rate (38.6%).

The Vikings’ unpredictable, overwhelming, exotic blitzes have tricked offenses so thoroughly that teams are frightened to run play-action passes, worried that quarterbacks momentarily turning their backs to the defense to sell the run fake could hinder their processing and lead to immediate negative plays.

Teams are averaging only a 19.3% play-action pass rate against Minnesota (31st), totaling just 40 such dropbacks. The Packers had 10 play-action dropbacks in Week 1 against the Vikings, and no offense has exceeded that total in a game since. The Saints and Colts combined for only six play-action dropbacks over the last two weeks. Meanwhile, the Lions’ offense ranks fourth this season with a 33.3% play-action pass rate and has recorded at least 11 such dropbacks in every game.

Against play-action passes this season, the Vikings’ defense is allowing 7.9 yards per attempt (19th), +0.003 EPA/dropback (12th), a 48.3% success rate (11th), and a staggering 13.8% explosive pass rate (27th). The inherent risk of turning your back to Minnesota’s defense and becoming the Headless Hurler is still real, as the Vikings have recorded a 16.2% sack rate (1st) and 48.6% pressure rate (1st) against play-action dropbacks.

The Vikings haven’t quite been tested against play action this season, with their matchup against the Bears coming in a monsoon, hardly a fair test of their passing attack. They’ll also face the Bills next week, an offense with the league’s second-highest play-action rate. While Minnesota remains formidable against play action, particularly with its ability to generate pressure and sacks, its defense ranks outside the top 10 in several metrics. It hasn’t been nearly as historically dominant against play action as it has against the run and on traditional dropbacks.

As Petzing illuminated last week, and as Lions fans have witnessed for years, Jared Goff is a different breed of beast as a precision processor when it comes to play-action passing. Detroit’s offensive line is also above average in pass protection, with room to improve as its younger players develop and the heady Cade Mays continues acclimating at the pivot. Now it’s a matter of proving they aren’t afraid of the dark when facing Minnesota’s pressure packages and are willing to challenge the Vikings with the play-action passing game that has been a staple of Detroit’s offense.

The Devil’s in the Dropback

Continuing on the topic of counterpunches to the Vikings flooding pass-rush lanes with second-level defenders such as Eric Wilson, Blake Cashman, the immortal Harrison Smith, and Josh Metellus. There’s another potential wrinkle for Detroit’s offense. It’s not often the Vikings are forced to defend straight dropbacks from under center. No team really is in this era of the NFL, but the Lions could be equipped to do it.

The Lions are averaging only 1.8 such dropbacks per game this season, but Jared Goff has completed 6-of-9 passes (66.7% completion percentage, 6th) for 84 yards (9.3 yards per attempt, 3rd) and two touchdowns (t-2nd). Detroit also ranks in the top 10 in success rate and explosive pass rate on under-center straight dropbacks, while its 4.7 yards after catch per attempt ranks fourth. They do need to be careful, however, as they’ve allowed a 40.0% quarterback pressure rate (7th) and one sack on these plays.

Luckily, straight dropbacks from under center have helped disarm the Vikings a bit. Flores’ furious, fully fanged forces have faced 15 under-center, non-play-action dropbacks this season (10th), allowing opponents to complete 9-of-14 passes (64.3% completion percentage, 6th) for 132 yards (9.4 yards per attempt)—nearly a first down per pass attempt, albeit on a small sample size! Minnesota also ranks in the bottom 10 in success rate and explosive pass rate allowed on these plays. Perhaps most surprisingly, they’ve generated pressure on just 13.3% of those dropbacks (t-27th).

The real treat is that the Vikings’ defense is allowing a league-worst 6.4 yards after catch per attempt on such passes. Perhaps all those aggressive, mugged-up looks at the line of scrimmage are proving hazardous, with defenders scrambling to get into coverage position after the snap and missing tackles.

This preview is about finding the small levers the Lions’ offense can pull against the most dangerous defense in the league. The Vikings’ pass defense feels inevitable. Stay on the field long enough, and they’ll get you. They’ll force you into mistakes.

Just like with play-action passes, straight dropbacks from under center offer a small avenue to exploit Minnesota’s aggression, get its defenders on their heels, and produce chunk plays. It’s an opportunity to move downfield quickly, catch Flores’ defense with its pants down, and get the ball into the hands of Detroit’s best playmakers with room to operate.

Ragnarök Meets Rah

Lions wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown can be a ghoul to opposing defenses. It’s part of why he’s a three-time consecutive All-Pro, and his hands, toughness, and consistency have helped him slay the Vikings in the past.

Over his last six games against the Vikings, St. Brown has averaged 10.8 targets, 8.3 receptions, 100.7 receiving yards, 0.5 touchdowns, and 5.1 first downs per game. That production is more menacingly consistent than Michael Myers terrorizing Haddonfield, Illinois. And as much as everyone loves Dr. Loomis, Flores might as well be playing his role, desperately trying and repeatedly failing to contain the Michael Myers of Detroit’s offense. 

Against the blitz this season, St. Brown has recorded 25 targets, 16 receptions, 204 receiving yards, three touchdowns, and 70 yards after catch. All five rank in the top 10 among wide receivers against the blitz. He’s been a ball magnet for Jared Goff when defenses bring extra rushers.

Last season, St. Brown was targeted 61 times against the blitz, hauling in 39 receptions (2nd) for 593 receiving yards (2nd), four touchdowns, and 329 yards after catch (1st). The Sun God has been Detroit’s secret weapon against the blitzkrieg.

As a secondary sidekick, while Sam LaPorta hasn’t experienced the same sustained success against the Vikings, he did record eight targets, six receptions, 97 receiving yards (16.2 yards per reception), one touchdown, and four first downs in his lone game against them last year. More importantly, LaPorta is eating blitzing defenses alive this season.

Against the blitz, LaPorta has recorded 14 targets, 11 receptions, 169 receiving yards (2nd among TEs), two touchdowns, and 92 yards after catch (4th among TEs). His 15.1 total receiving EPA ranks second among tight ends and fifth among all players.

Between St. Brown and LaPorta, Goff has a pair of boogeymen capable of giving Flores’ defense a taste of its own nightmare fuel.

This is my Boomstick

You can’t run and you can’t hide from the Vikings’ defense when you’re trying to run from under center, as Minnesota leads the NFL in EPA/rush allowed (-0.26) and rushing success rate allowed (27.8%), among a litany of other metrics in this category.

However, they’ve gotten their teeth kicked in against 34 shotgun runs this season:

  • 6.35 yards per carry (31st)
  • +0.24 EPA/rush (30th)
  • 58.8% rushing success rate allowed
  • 1.56 yards before contact per carry (17th)
  • 4.79 yards after contact per carry (32nd)
  • 11.1% stuff rate (28th)
  • 11.8% explosive run rate (17th)

The stats are so stark that they’re almost unrecognizable as belonging to the same Vikings defense.

On shotgun runs this season, Jahmyr Gibbs has rushed 17 times for 89 yards (5.24 yards per carry) and an impressive 2.41 yards before contact per rush. He’s also been one of the most effective running backs on man-scheme runs from shotgun, with seven carries for 49 yards (7.0 yards per carry) and a league-leading 3.57 yards before contact per attempt. He’s recorded three runs of 10-plus yards (1st) and forced two missed tackles on those attempts.

It’s a small sample size, but it’s yet another chainsaw for Drew Petzing and the Lions’ offense to wield Flores’ way. Get Gibbs in shotgun looks, let his offensive line pulverize an unprepared defensive front, and let Gibbs do the rest.

Night of The Living Linemen

While on the topic of those physically imposing offensive linemen up front, Detroit’s unit still has plenty of imperfections, but like Frankenstein’s monster, it’s been pieced together and brought back to life. It’s important to remind Lions fans just how far this group has come from last year’s makeshift offensive line, particularly the units tasked with protecting Jared Goff and opening up escape routes for Jahmyr Gibbs against the Vikings’ defense.

Lions Offensive Line — 2025 Weeks 9, 17 vs. Minnesota (snaps played)

  • Tate Ratledge — 123
  • Penei Sewell — 122
  • Christian Mahogany — 121
  • Dan Skipper — 78
  • Kingsley Eguakun — 64
  • Graham Glasgow — 64
  • Taylor Decker — 54

item.title: 3 things Cowboys HC Brian Schottenheimer can carry into week 8
item.description: How much do you trust Brian Schottenheimer right now?
item.content:encoded:
It has been a bumpy ride so far in 2026 for Brian Schottenheimer. The inconsistency and lack of plan has been on display way too much this year, but there were some things that Schottenheimer should be able to carry into week eight that could help the Cowboys win back-to-back games for the first time in 2026.

1) Commitment to the run

For the first time this season, the Cowboys showed a commitment to the running game in their 38-21 win against the Eagles.

Despite that being a big talking point so far this season, the Cowboys running game hasn’t been good enough to fully commit too, especially when they have been trailing as much as they have. But all things seemed to click on the ground for the Cowboys against the Eagles, and they should be able to carry those things into their matchup against the Cardinals.

Against the Eagles, we saw a lot more creativity with the running game, using pin/pulls, traps, and misdirection to create explosive runs rather consistently. The Cardinals defense has been pretty successful so far this season defending the run, ranking sixth in rush EPA/play and 20th in rush success rate. Despite the Cardinals run rankings so far this year, the Cowboys should be able to have a solid night again on the ground if they commit to it and use similar creativity that they did in Week 7 against the Eagles.

2) Continue to push the ball down the field

One of the major changes in the offense we saw last week was their aggressiveness to push the ball down the field in the passing game. After six weeks of seeing Dak Prescott’s ADOT rank near the bottom of the league, the Cowboys generated explosive plays at an extremely high clip against a defense that had not given up many explosive passing plays to start the season.

With so many defenses sitting on the stop-routes that have been in heavy rotation to start the year, the Cowboys were able to hit multiple big plays using sluggos on the outside, which should be there for them yet again against a Cardinals secondary that has struggled to slow down opposing passing games in 2026 (31st in dropback epa/play and 20th in dropback success rate).

3) More Brevyn Spann-Ford

After signing an early contract extension this offseason, their has been a lot of talk about the Cowboys showcasing Spann-Ford more and having him cut into Jake Ferguson’s snaps.

Over the last two weeks, that has started to happen. Spann-Ford will likely never be a dynamic receiver, but he offers enough there to lead the team in snaps played at tight end given his blocking ability and ability to pickup yards after the catch with his physical style of play.

Spann-Ford opens a lot of things up for the Cowboys running game that wouldn’t be there with Ferguson in the lineup in 11-personnel. The different looks both with the pass and the run they can give defenses when in 12-personnel makes him a very valuable piece to this Cowboys offense moving forward.
