item.title: Ed Oliver’s return can help unlock Bills defense
item.description: Buffalo’s defense should get a big boost from Oliver’s return
item.content:encoded:
There has been much conversation around the defensive play of the Buffalo Bills this season and the shortcomings under new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard. While many Bills fans have been frustrated, myself included, there is one piece of the equation that has not been discussed enough this season.

Thanks to multiple injuries, star defensive tackle Ed Oliver has only appeared in three games for Buffalo this season. Oliver missed week two after suffering a hip injury in warm-ups, and then excited the game early after taking a shot to his left knee during week 4. Much of the focus on the defense’s shortcoming have been centered around the play of the secondary and linebacker corps, I would argue that Oliver’s absence has had the greater impact.

Statistically speaking, the Bills defense has performed at a higher level with Oliver on the field. The team has given up 25.3 points per game when Oliver plays, compared to 31.7 per game when he does not. The Bills also allow less yards per game when Oliver plays, and have 17 quarterback pressures during those games (as opposed to six total in the three games he missed). Looking past the statistics, it should also be noted that opposing offenses have marched down the field late in games to score late touchdowns in games that have been missed by Oliver (Los Angeles Rams, Las Vegas Raiders, and after exiting against the New England Patriots).

If you want to take it one step further, Oliver’s absence seems to be having an adverse affect on the play of Greg Rousseau. In games played by Oliver, fans saw Rousseau tally four sacks to go along with six tackles for a loss. Without Oliver proves to be another story, where Rousseau did not have any tackles for loss in those games. There has also been an impact on Deone Walker as Oliver has missed time, with the second-year defensive tackle being double-teamed on 71% of defensive snaps.

While much of the conversation has focused on the secondary, I am optimistic that the anticipated return of Oliver will provide a much needed jolt for the Bills defense on Sunday. Let’s hope that I am right as the Bills face a tough challenge against Lamar Jackson and the Baltimore Ravens.

item.title: As the trade deadline approaches, should Browns listen to Jared Verse offers?
item.description: The Cleveland Browns new pass rusher isn’t getting to the quarterback. Should Jared Verse be on the trade block?
item.content:encoded:
This time during the NFL season, two things are the most topical: Game results each weekend and the looming NFL trade deadline.

The Cleveland Browns have gotten off to a great start with a 5-2-0 record. Could a trade help this roster, or perhaps the Browns should sit tight and ride with what brought them.

RELATED: VERSE UNAFRAID TO TALK DESPITE ZERO SACKS

The NFL trade deadline is November 10. The league instituted a deadline for teams to prevent clubs from stacking rosters right before the playoffs and keep competitive balance towards the end of the season.

This year’s trade deadline has generated a lot of interest in the defensive line. This market has already begun. The Indianapolis Colts traded DE DeForest Buckner back to the San Francisco 49ers. The Tennessee Titans traded star DL Jeffery Simmons to the Chicago Bears.

The Browns’ pass rush is not getting quick pressure from the defensive ends this year and hasn’t been the same since the team traded away All-World pass rusher Myles Garrett. In that trade, Cleveland received Jared Verse, who had gone to two Pro Bowls in two seasons, and was voted the “NFL Defensive Rookie of the Year” when he came into the league in 2024.

The idea was that Verse would fill in for Garrett, but not take his place.

In just seven games, the Browns have 20 sacks collectively. Verse has zero. This is a guy who had 7.5 last year and 4.5 as a rookie.

What exactly is wrong with Verse? Should the Browns coaching staff keep waiting for him to blow up the opposition during passing plays? Is there a scheme or fit issue?

Or maybe, should Cleveland make him available before the trade deadline?

Well-Versed

For months since the Garrett trade, all we have heard is that Verse wasn’t going to fill Garrett’s shoes, but was an exceptional athlete and would provide a very good pass rush. 

While with the Los Angeles Rams, Verse had 58 tackles last year and 66 the year before. Ink noted that he was a good run stopper, along with his sack numbers and his ability to get into the backfield and hunt quarterbacks. 27 QB hits in 2025, along with 36 pressures. And that Verse is a much younger version of Garrett, being just 25 years old.

And yet, here are his stats for this year: Seven starts, 302 defensive snaps,17 total tackles (2.4 on average per game), 4 tackles for loss, 5 QB hits, 0 sacks, 0 forced fumbles, 0 fumble recoveries, 0 batted passes, 0 hurries, 4 knockdowns, 4 pressures, and 3 missed tackles.

Other than tackles, he isn’t averaging one of anything per game.

This year’s version of the Browns defense, coached by DC Mike Rutenberg, keeps receiving praise week after week. Just not the edge rush portion.

On the other side, the Browns lost DE Alex Wright for the year after he was placed on season–ending IR after suffering a ruptured Achilles tendon during training camp. In his place came Isaiah McGuire, who isn’t a better pass rusher or run stopper, with Derek Barnett as his backup.

Verse just isn’t getting into the other team’s offensive backfield whatsoever. Plus, he is weak at staying home and offering containment. On occasion, Verse will do this unusual maneuver where he won’t go directly towards the quarterback, but will travel towards the center and then take a hard right. And it’s not like he is playing full games. Currently, his snap count is just 66% of all defensive reps.  

His pressure rate has dropped significantly this year to just 6.6%, which ranks him #71 among all NFL EDGE rushers. Verse posted a 16.8% pressure rate during the 2025 season while playing for the Rams. His Pro Football Focus pass-rushing grade was 82.2, which ranked him #13. That has sunk to 59.9, which is #73 among 113 qualified EDGE defenders.

Needless to say, the Cleveland version of Verse is not the Los Angeles edition the Browns were anticipating. Nobody expected Verse to ball out for 20 sacks, but geez. What is going on?

Perhaps it surrounds the fact that Verse came from a 3-4 alignment while with the Rams and is now grouped in the 4-3. Sounds logical, right? This has led to offensive tackles neutralizing his power-first and bull-rush moves. And earlier in the season, because of his reputation, teams were double-teaming him. But that suddenly ceased as offensive coordinators realized it wasn’t necessary.

And while Verse has struggled, his backup, Sam Williams, has played pretty well in spite of getting just 36% of defensive snaps while playing part-time.

Williams has played in all seven games with zero starts, and has 20 total tackles, 5 tackles for loss, 1 sack, 3 QB hits, 0 forced fumbles, 0 fumble recoveries, 1 batted pass, 1 hurry, 2 knockdowns, 4 pressures, and 4 missed tackles.

Unthinkable decision?

The league has several pass rushers that are projected to be traded soon. The market for defensive linemen has already begun. The only other pass rushers rumored to be traded, at least as of now, before the November 10 deadline are Los Angeles Chargers EDGE rusher Khalil Mack and Josh Sweat of the Arizona Cardinals.

Should the Browns throw Verse’s name into the hat and see if anyone bites? Would the team jump at a strong offer?

Verse is one of those EDGE rushers who has had good to very good numbers every year on a consistent basis, but he isn’t going to blow the doors off. This year, his production is more often viewed as mediocre to poor.

Then there is the money issue. Verse is in the third year of a four-year $15.1 million deal, with all of it guaranteed. This year he has a cap hit of $2.2 million. Next year that increases to $2.9 million.

Next season, the Browns will need to make a decision on Verse’s fifth-year option. That is currently projected to be a fully guaranteed $27.9 million that would be paid in 2028. Verse qualifies for the largest tier as a multi-time Pro Bowler.

But there is a hitch: he isn’t playing at that high level. His production is way down. Yes, the Browns could stick it out and see if this is just a one-off, or perhaps he will wake up and produce in the second half of this season. Because Verse was a part of the Garrett trade, everyone has had high expectations for him. This year.

Cleveland has a timeline, and currently Verse is included in that plan. Some media folks have pointed out that his presence along the defensive line during passing downs has generated sacks and stats for other Browns defensive players. That rings true in a lot of games across the league. Often, a player will engage two offensive linemen so that another defender can loop around and get to the quarterback on a stunt.

For now, everyone is waiting for Verse to show why he was the necessary piece in the Garrett trade. Every team in the NFL is looking for an EDGE rusher.

The big question for Cleveland GM Andrew Berry: Which is better for the Browns this year and in following seasons? Have Jared Verse on the roster, or have whichever rookie player they select with whatever draft pick(s) they would receive in a trade?

item.title: 5 Ravens to zero-in on vs. Bills
item.description: Baltimore needs a win this week to keep pace in the crowded AFC playoff race
item.content:encoded:
The Buffalo Bills are set to host the Baltimore Ravens this weekend in a tough matchup that could have playoff implications. Buffalo is vying for the No. 1 seed in the AFC, and they currently sit two games up in the loss column on the New England Patriots in the AFC East. Baltimore, on the other hand, is currently in fourth place in the AFC North, but at 4-3, they are firmly involved in the AFC playoff picture.

While the Bills and the Ravens may not be divisional foes, they very well could find themselves fighting for seeding once January hits. A head-to-head victory not only helps Buffalo maintain their divisional lead, but it could also make a big difference in their playoff path.

Baltimore isn’t a typical last-place team; they are far too talented to be taken lightly, and the Bills know they have a fight on their hands this week. If they want to earn a win this Sunday, they’ll need to account for these five avens to watch.
_____________________________________________________________________________

QB Lamar Jackson

After missing the last three games with an ankle injury, Jackson is poised to return, and just in time for the Ravens. Baltimore is always dangerous, but with Jackson back, an already dangerous offense becomes a big challenge for a struggling Buffalo defense.

The Bills have traditionally hemmed Jackson in fairly well, but with a new coordinator and a new scheme on the defensive side, there’s no way to know if that success will translate this year. So far, Buffalo’s defense has had next to no success, as they sit 30th in points allowed and 31st in yards allowed this season. If Jackson’s mobility is limited, it could limit his effectiveness, as he consistently makes huge plays with his legs. While Jackson is perfectly capable of beating teams from the pocket, Buffalo has to force him to stay there and make him do it for four quarters.

WR Zay Flowers

After signing a big extension this offseason, Baltimore’s top receiver has justified that deal with a huge start to the season. Flowers has 40 catches for 608 yards and three touchdowns on 53 targets. He can operate from the outside and from the slot. He has tremendous speed, he runs great routes, and he can attack the defense at every level. In short, he’s a nightmare for a struggling pass defense like Buffalo’s.

Hell, he’s a tough cover for anyone. After watching Christian Benford travel with Brock Bowers last week, it wouldn’t surprise me at all to see him draw the same assignment for Flowers. Benford can use his size and length—he’s 6’1” with 31” or 32” long arms, depending on the source—to jam the 5’9” Flowers at the line. Physicality is going to be the name of the game this week, as giving Flowers a free release is a recipe for disaster. Limiting him and making Jackson look elsewhere will be a key part of the game plan on Sunday.

LB Roquan Smith

The veteran is still one of the best in the game, and this seaosn, he’s performed better in coverage than he has at any point in his career. So far, he’s allowing just 53.8% of passes thrown his way to be completed; opposing quarterbacks have a rating of just 56.3 when targeting Smith in the passing game. Those numbers are both career bests for the 29-year old five-time All-Pro. Normally, I’d say he’s someone to target in the passing game, as he allows better than a 70% completion rate against for his career.

And, while I think that the Raven will use Kyle Hamilton to guard Buffalo’s tight ends over the middle, they could very well use Smith to do that if he’s matched up agaisnt someone like Dawson Knox or Jackson Hawes. Smith is also big enough and physical enough to act as a spy on quarterback Josh Allen, and while he has dealt with a knee injury, he seems ready to return to a full-time role this weekend. Keeping track of No. 0 has to be a big part of Sunday’s plan on offense.

S Kyle Hamilton

The versatile defensive back is always worth watching, as he has the toughness to erase tight ends and the quickness to deal with most wide receivers over the middle. Hamilton is a long, sturdy defender who can neutralize even high-end talents; however, he’s been limited a bit of late thanks to a lingering knee issue. He sat out of Wednesday’s practice before logging a limited session Thursday and a full session on Friday. He enters the game without an injury designation, but he hasn’t quite been as dominant in the early going of this season as he has been in years past.

He’s allowing 67.9% of passes to be completed when he’s the closest man in coverage, and he’s allowing a career-high 8.9 yards per completion. He’s also missed five tackles so far this season, and his missed tackle percentage so far is a career-high 9.1%. Sure, opposing quarterbacks have just an 80.8 quarterback rating when targeting him, but for a three-time All-Pro, it’s a small step in the wrong direction. I assume that Hamilton’s main mark will be Dalton Kincaid this week, who is questionable to play thanks to a chest injury. If Buffalo has Kincaid, Khalil Shakir, and DJ Moore, then Hamilton can’t erase all of them. Whichever player he’s on should be targeted with caution, but there will be opportunities for Buffalo over the middle.

CB Nate Wiggins

With all due respect to veteran Marlon Humphrey, it’s Wiggins who is their top corner, in my eyes. Wiggins has allowed just 55.6% of passes thrown his way to be completed; he has four pass breakups on the season to give him 31 in 39 career games. Despite how talented Wiggins is, he was repeatedly abused by Josh Allen and the Bills during last season’s wild 41-40 comeback victory.

Allen targeted Wiggins’ man seven times, completing six of those passes for 78 yards. Allen was outstanding that night, throwing for 394 yards and two touchdowns while completing 33-of-46 passes. Wiggins is too good to take lightly, however, and he’ll likely be matched up against either Keon Coleman or DJ Moore. Buffalo can’t ignore those guys, so they’ll need to win their reps against Wiggins in order to give the Bills a chance at victory.

item.title: Jonathan Taylor trade talks are "active and ongoing"
item.description: Seahawks, Packers, Broncos, Vikings, Giants are pegged as potential destinations.
item.content:encoded:
There are two ways to handle the trade of a cornerstone player. One, talk quietly to a minimal number of teams. Like the Titans did with defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons. Two, throw the doors open and try to get the best possible package of draft picks and/or players in return. Like the Colts are now doing with running back Jonathan Taylor.

Indianapolis has officially declared that Taylor is available, via a selective and strategic leak to ESPNFL. Trade talks are "active and ongoing," per the report.

The teams that have "expressed at least some level of interest" are the Broncos, Packers, Vikings, Giants, and Seahawks.

Last weekend's Sunday Splash! report that operated as the "everything must go" sign for the Colts pegged the Broncos, Packers, Vikings, and Seahawks as potentially interested teams in Taylor. The Giants (who are believed, we're told by multiple sources, to have been pursuing Simmons) are a new arrival. Which would possibly be bad news for second-year running back Cam Skattebo, who emerged from the doghouse last week with 124 rushing yards. (It wouldn't be a surprise if the Giants offered Skattebo to the Colts as part of the trade package, frankly.)

To the extent that tying four teams to the trade talks doesn't get the Colts maximum compensation, the new report notes that the Colts "would prefer" that Taylor stick around for their "rebuild."

If they really wanted Taylor, they wouldn't be fielding trade offers fo him.

The Colts reportedly are looking for a package similar to what the 49ers sent to the Panthers in 2022 for running back Christian McCaffrey: a second-round pick, a third-round pick, and a fourth-round pick in the 2023 draft and a fifth-round pick in the 2024 draft.

The next question is whether Taylor will play on Sunday. It's possible, in our view, the Colts will hold Taylor out of action on Sunday at Jacksonville, like the Cardinals did three weeks ago when they had a deal in place to trade receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. to the Texans. Even without a deal, keeping Taylor out of the game would ensure that he won't get injured.

If that happens, rookie Seth McGowan would be the likely starter in Week 8. Last Sunday, the seventh-rounder who played for Kentucky last year had 11 carries for 48 yards in a 16-10 loss to the Vikings.

And the Vikings continue to make the most sense for Taylor. Especially since they had the best possible opportunity to scout him six days ago, when he had 18 carries for 95 yards and an Adrian Peterson-style 38-yard touchdown run.

If the Vikings add Taylor in the coming days, he'd likely make his debut as soon as next Monday night, when the Vikings host the Bills. And when they put Peterson in the team's Ring of Honor.

item.title: Future Broncos: A 2027 NFL Mock Draft for Denver
item.description: Mile High Report’s Christopher Hart gives his first 2027 NFL Mock draft for the Denver Broncos.
item.content:encoded:
Happy Halloween, Broncos Country. The end of October is here, and the halfway point of college football season is upon us. That makes it the right time to do my annual Mocktober installment for my Future Broncos series.

The Broncos are projected to have nine picks in the 2027 NFL Draft. It’s expected they will earn a fourth-round compensatory pick for John Franklin-Myers. Additionally, they’ll receive a seventh-round pick from the Saints to finalize the Devaughn Vele trade.

Based on their current record and strength of schedule, the Broncos are slated to pick 27th next April. This is sort of no man’s land for picking in the first round. I used Pro Football Network’s mock draft simulator to help with the exercise, used their consensus board for player rankings, and adhered to their trade calculator. And yes—I did make two big trades to get playmakers for Denver.

27th Overall, First Round — Carter Smith, OT — Indiana

I’ve discussed several first-round options for the Broncos in earlier segments such as Ole Miss defensive tackle Will Echoles, Oregon tight end Jamari Johnson, Minnesota offensive lineman Greg Johnson, and Georgia linebacker Chris Cole. None of them were available when I was on the clock.

That being said, I still view offensive line as a premier need for Denver. Garett Bolles and Mike McGlinchey won’t be around forever. Plus, the Broncos could use more talent across the board. This pick might probably will come off as a mild reach to a lot of folks, but Indiana offensive tackle Carter Smith would be a good selection for the Broncos. I think he is a prospect who will gain a lot of steam leading up to April.

Smith (6’5”, 310 pounds) has manned down the Hoosiers left tackle position since 2023. Playing over 3,000 snaps, he boasts a lot of experience and will finish his decorated collegiate career with over 50 starts at the position. His coaches laud him for his leadership and toughness. Moreover, the tape shows a player who is disciplined and is great at pass protection and run blocking.

The big question surrounding Smith, as well as some other top offensive linemen in this year’s class, is if they have the requisite length to stick at tackle instead of moving to the outside. That doesn’t concern me too much, because his technique is outstanding.

Head Coach Sean Payton has continuously stated he values experience and positional versatility when scouting offensive lineman. Smith checks all those boxes and gives the Broncos a potential high-end starter at multiple positions. What’s not to like?

47th Overall, Second Round — Luke Reynolds, Tight End — Virginia Tech

It wouldn’t be a fun Halloween mock draft without projecting the trade. In this scenario, I have Denver sending their second-round selection (#59), their fourth-round compensatory pick for Franklin-Myers (#135), and a future fourth-round pick in 2028 to the Dallas Cowboys. It seems like a logical move, since the Cowboys could use a little bit more draft capital.

Finding an impact tight end is a big desire for Broncos Country. A player I discussed early on in the process was Virginia Tech tight end Luke Reynolds. I predicted back in September he would gain steam and wind up being a Top 50 selection. I still think that happens.

The junior standout has continued to play at a high level. He now has 50 catches, 493 receiving yards, and 6 touchdowns in eight games for the Hokies. Overall, Reynolds is well-rounded player that can make a difference inline a run blocker and be versatile and legitimate threat in Denver’s passing game.

Last year, over half a dozen went off on the board during Day 2. If Denver wants to upgrade the position via the draft, they’ll have to make a move early on to get one of the best prospects. I think sending off a few extra Day 3 picks to snag a prospect of Reynolds’ caliber would be well worth it.

60th Overall, Second Round — Reed Harris, WR — Arizona State

Now, the fun is just getting started. Perhaps you think it’s not realistic to see Denver be big time draft day movers up the board twice on Day 2. After all, Denver has maneuvered down the board recently. They basically had to since they’ve been without first round picks for three of five seasons and needed to recoup ammo.

That’s all fine and dandy, but let’s face it—finding a potential replacement for Courtland Sutton has to be on their radar. He hasn’t made much of a difference this year at all. Moreover, he carries a substantial cap hit next season. Though that’s not the only reason they should make an early investment at the position.

Jaylen Waddle hasn’t made a big impact in his first season with the team. Unfortunately, Pat Bryant has been injured, Marvin Mims Jr. is a free agent, and next year is the last of Troy Franklin’s rookie contract. I have no doubt the Broncos’ brass will be looking to add more weapons to improve their offensive production. They need a needle mover at the position.

For this trade, I sent #92 in the third round, #162 in the fifth round, a 2028 third-round pick to snag #60 from the Cleveland Browns. That’s a big price to pay, but to target a player who is a favorite fit of mine for Denver, I felt it was worth it.

Earlier this month, I highlighted Arizona State wide receiver Reed Harris. He has continued to impress since then and now has 47 catches for a conference leading 800 receiving yards and 8 touchdowns. Harris is coming off a 6 catch, 147-yard performance against Kansas State last Saturday.

There’s no doubt #3 is easily one of the best contested catch and deep ball receivers in this year’s draft. He lines up with Payton’s size desires (6’5”, 220 pounds) and would give Denver a dynamic threat who could help them out immediately as a rookie.

Quite honestly, he likely won’t be on the board late in the second round. But for the purposes of this exercise, I had to pounce when I saw he was still available. Three picks in, three long-term issues addressed on offense which has been Denver’s biggest issue in 2026.

Day 3 Selections

128th Overall, Fourth Round: Jyaire Hill, CB — Michigan

Hill has been a mainstay in the Wolverines secondary the past three seasons and a productive player. In over thirty games as a starter, the senior standout has 112 tackles, 11 tackles for loss, 2 sacks, and 3 interceptions. I was surprised he was ranked so lowly on their board.

He’s got good size (6’2″, 190 pounds) and covers well from both man and zone. I think he’s a good fit for Vance Joseph’s defense with true boundary potential. Adding to the secondary makes sense with a lot of starting players with their contracts running out in the next two seasons.

208th Overall, Sixth Round:Drayk Bowen, LB — Notre Dame

Bowen has been a productive starting linebacker for the Fighting Irish. He has played in 47 games and notched 197 tackles, 10 tackles for loss, and 4.5 sacks to date. He won’t be a premier playmaker in coverage, but his high football IQ, toughness in run support, and special team’s ability would make him a valuable addition to Denver’s linebacking corps. He reminds me quite a bit of Josey Jewell.

229th Overall, Seventh Round (via New Orleans):Sheridan Wilson, C — Texas Tech

Wilson is a fifth-year senior who has started at the pivot for the Red Raiders since 2024. He will finish his collegiate career with nearly 3,000 snaps. As noted earlier, Payton values experience and Wilson has a lot of it. He is also regarded as one of the best pass blocking centers in this year’s class. With Alex Forsyth in the last year of his contract and Luke Wattenberg’s up-and-down play, finding a developmental prospect at center would be wise for the Broncos.

245th Overall, Seventh Round: Dallas Afalava, DT — Wake Forest

Afalava started his career at Idaho, but took his talents to Wake Forest to battle tougher talent in the ACC. At 6’2” and 295 pounds, he isn’t the biggest defensive lineman. However, he makes up for that being quick disrupter off the line of scrimmage. The Demon Deacons move him all over their defensive front and his low center of gravity and initial burst give opposing offensive lineman fits. He is also a core special team’s player for them. I’m always in favor of adding competition to the trenches.

What do you think, Broncos Country?

Would you be a fan of a draft like this for the Broncos? If not, who are some of the players that are high on your wish list for Denver in the 2027 NFL Draft? Let me know in the comments section.

item.title: Chicago Bears Week 8 Flashbacks: A Pair of Walk Offs and a Franchise Record
item.description: Hop aboard the Gridiron Time Machine with @iamcogs and take a trip down Week 8 Bears memory lane!
item.content:encoded:
We’re already nearly half way through the 2026 NFL season, in the blink of an eye at that! But that doesn’t slow this time machine, let’s take a look at three more SPoooooooKY games from the Bears past! Happy Halloween!

1. 2005, Bears @ Lions: Peanut walks it off in overtime

October 30, 2005 | Bears win 19-13 (OT)

The 2005 Bears were still finding their identity when they traveled to Detroit for a Week 8 matchup with significant implications for the NFC North standings.

Chicago entered at 3-3, tied with Detroit for first place in the division.

Rookie quarterback Kyle Orton put together one of his better performances of the season, completing 17-of-31 passes for a career-high 230 yards and a touchdown. His 23-yard scoring strike to Muhsin Muhammad capped a 99-yard touchdown drive, helping Chicago build a 13-3 halftime lead.

Detroit battled back, tying the game at 13 early in the fourth quarter. Neither offense could break the deadlock, sending the game into overtime.

That’s when Charles Tillman decided he’d seen enough.

Lions quarterback Jeff Garcia rolled to his right before attempting an ill-advised throw back across the field toward Mike Williams. Tillman stepped in front of the pass and raced 22 yards for the game-winning touchdown.

Chicago improved to 4-3, taking sole possession of first place in the NFC North.

The victory also carried historical significance, as the Bears became the first franchise in NFL history to reach 650 regular-season victories.

2. 2006, Bears vs. 49ers: Chicago scores 41 points before halftime

October 29, 2006 | Bears win 41-10

The 2006 Bears entered Week 8 undefeated, having survived their unforgettable Monday Night Football comeback against Arizona two weeks earlier.

Apparently, they were interested in making this one a little less stressful.

Chicago welcomed San Francisco to Soldier Field and proceeded to put together one of the most dominant first halves in franchise history.

The Bears scored 24 points in the opening quarter alone, establishing a franchise record for first-quarter scoring. By halftime, Chicago had built an absolutely ridiculous 41-0 advantage.

Quarterback Rex Grossman rebounded from his disastrous outing against Arizona, completing 23-of-29 passes for 252 yards, three touchdowns and no interceptions. His 137.4 passer rating was among his best performances of the season.

Tight end Desmond Clark caught six passes for 86 yards and two touchdowns, while Thomas Jones contributed 111 rushing yards and another score.

The defense was equally impressive.

Brian Urlacher delivered one of the afternoon’s most memorable plays, batting an Alex Smith pass into the air before securing a remarkable one-handed interception.

Chicago forced four first-half turnovers, converting each into a touchdown.

The 41 first-half points tied a franchise record established against Washington in 1948. The Bears eventually cruised to a 41-10 victory, improving to 7-0 for the first time since their legendary 1985 season.

3. 2012, Bears vs. Panthers: Cutler and Gould pull off a Halloween miracle

October 28, 2012 | Bears win 23-22

The 2012 Bears entered Week 8 riding a four-game winning streak and sitting comfortably atop the NFC North at 5-1.

For three quarters against Carolina, however, Chicago looked nothing like a division leader.

The Panthers thoroughly dominated the Bears, building a 19-7 advantage while making life miserable for Jay Cutler.

Cutler was sacked six times in the first half alone, throwing an interception and losing two fumbles. At one point late in the third quarter, Carolina had outgained Chicago 369-59.

Then things got weird.

With just under seven minutes remaining, Cutler connected with Kellen Davis for a 12-yard touchdown, trimming Carolina’s lead to 19-14.

Eight seconds later, the Bears were winning.

On Carolina’s very next offensive snap, receiver Steve Smith slipped while running his route, allowing Tim Jennings to intercept Cam Newton and return the football 25 yards for a touchdown.

Chicago had somehow scored two touchdowns in eight seconds.

The Panthers weren’t finished, though, reclaiming a 22-20 lead on a 45-yard field goal with 2:27 remaining.

That left Cutler one final opportunity.

He completed six of seven passes for 52 yards on the ensuing possession, including several crucial completions to Brandon Marshall, setting up Robbie Gould for a 41-yard field goal as time expired.

Good as Gould. Bears win, 23-22.

Cutler finished 19-of-28 for 186 yards, one touchdown and one interception. Marshall caught nine passes for 98 yards, while Jennings recorded two interceptions, including the game-changing pick-six.

Chicago improved to 6-1 despite being outgained 416-210.

Gary Baugher Jr. is a second year contributor to WCG, bringing football insight backed by over 16 years of experience in organized football and more than 30 years as a passionate fan of the game. You can follow him on Twitter at @iamcogs.

item.title: Washington Commanders vs Philadelphia Eagles Week 8: Five Questions with Bleeding Green Nation
item.description: Which team is more desperate for a win?
item.content:encoded:
It’s week 8 of the NFL season and the 1-4-1 Washington Commanders will be facing a 2-5 Eagles team at home at Northwest Stadium on Saturday at 8:20 p.m. ET. The Eagles started the season with two straight wins, but have since lost their last 5 games. I covered the overview of the Eagles in the week 1 matchup article, so I won’t rehash the same points here except for the basics. Instead, I’ll focus on what has changed.

On offense, Eagles QB Jalen Hurts will miss the season due to blood clots and is replaced by backup Tanner McKee. McKee is a 3rd-year NFL player who is more of a traditional pocket passer than the athletic Hurts. Although McKee has played well in limited action prior to this year, the Eagles traded for Andy Dalton this past offseason and made him the immediate backup to Hurts. Dalton’s poor play in limited action week 3 led to Dalton being demoted and McKee seeing the field when Hurts was eventually ruled unfit to play, though it’s a reasonable question if the offseason moves may have hurt his confidence. Another big change in the Eagles since week 1 is the fast that almost their entire offensive line has been reconfigured multiple times. RT Lane Johnson retired (replaced by 2026 3rd-round pick Markel Bell), C Cam Jurgens was traded, and LG Landon Dickerson was out with injury and is now back. WRs Devonta Smith and Dontavion Wicks are also out for this game due to injury, leaving a lot of the receiving game in the hands of 2026 1st-round pick Makai Lemon.

On defense, the Eagles are healthier, primarily dealing with injury to LB Jihaad Campbell, who has been ruled out of week 8. Despite their health, the Eagles defense has declined precipitously in 2026 to be the 5th-worst pass defense by yards allowed and the 6th-worst rush defense by yards allowed, as well as ranking poorly in advanced stats. One theory behind the defense’s decline is that they are getting beat up from being on the field all the time due to the collapse of the offense. Through Week 7, the Eagles defense has been on the field for 67.3 plays/game, 4th-most in the NFL. Certain players have had a harder time than others, with slot CB Cooper DeJean suffering from a high missed-tackle rate and notable drop in coverage quality.

I asked Brandon Lee Gowton of Bleeding Green Nation five questions to better understand the state of the Eagles and what to look for in this game.

1) What has changed for the Eagles since the last time these teams faced off? Let’s exclude the Jalen Hurts situation from this, since it requires a lot of nuance and has been covered elsewhere.

Might be more efficient to list what hasn’t changed.

BGN alumnus Jimmy Kempski put together an “Eagles season from hell tracker” which details all the crazy stuff that’s been going on. 

In broader strokes, the offense has been really bad and ineffective. These struggles can be explained in part due to Lane Johnson unexpectedly retiring and the Eagles getting hit hard by injuries. But it’s hard to argue the coaching staff has made the most out of the talent they’ve been given to work with. The offense did show some signs of life against the Cowboys in Week 7 … but the Dallas defense is pretty awful, so, it’s hard to know how much of that success will carry over moving forward.

The Eagles’ defense, which was supposed to be their biggest strength this season, has underperformed lofty expectations. They’re coming off their worst (or second-worst) performance of the 2026 campaign after getting bullied by the Cowboys on Monday night. The Eagles have poured way too many resources into their defensive front to be as ineffective as they were against Dallas. They didn’t make Dak Prescott look the slightest bit uncomfortable, logging zero quarterback hits. And the Eagles also got shoved around in the run game.

It’s hardly hyperbolic to qualify the Eagles as one of the worst teams in the NFL right now. They rank bottom five in DVOA, point differential, and weighted EPA per play on both offense and defense.

2) Will the Eagles be sellers or buyers at the trade deadline or stand pat (and why)? If they make trades, what kind of trades would you foresee?

They SHOULD be sellers. This isn’t a season worth salvaging.

This isn’t to suggest Howie Roseman should be selling players for merely whatever they can get for them. The price has to be right in each deal. But I expect the Eagles to be receiving offers that will be worth their while.

There are different groups of players that the Eagles could be looking to sell. Some are in the no-brainer category in terms of players who are entering contract seasons and don’t figure to be long-term pieces in Philly. Those guys include the likes of Moro Ojomo, Riq Woolen, Dallas Goedert.

And then there are bigger names like Saquon Barkley (whose situation could be complicated by injury issues) and Zack Baun. Again, I’d be surprised if the Eagles unload those guys unless the price is simply too good to turn down, as was the case with the Cam Jurgens trade.

The Eagles shouldn’t be opposed to buying if there’s value to be had in acquiring a player who projects to be a long-term contributor. But there’s no need for any short-term rentals.

3) Eagles fans have made a lot of Nick Sirianni’s winning percentage, but what does he do to contribute to that winning percentage and how much do you think he deserves credit for it vs roster talent, a great DC, etc? Will he be around next year?

In fairness, it is a pretty crazy winning percentage. 9 of the 11 head coaches who currently rank ahead of him are in the Pro Football Hall of Fame.

The question you pose is fair. As a Sirianni skeptic, I can struggle to see the value he brings to the table. And I think this season is really bearing out the idea that he’s been heavily carried by elite general managing and a great defensive coordinator. With those two aspects not being as strong this season as they have in the past, the team suddenly looks a lot worse as Sirianni struggles to provide answers to persisting problems.

Perhaps I’m underestimating the significance of Sirianni having multiple years on his contract left but I struggle to see him back next year based on Jeffrey Lurie’s precedent of not tolerating offensive struggles. Three of the Eagles’ worst offensive seasons in this century were 2012, 2015, and 2020. What happened after each of those years? The head coach was fired. The Eagles had another one of those very bad offensive years in 2025 … but the team understandably didn’t want to fire their head coach one year after winning the Super Bowl. But is Lurie really going to tolerate another season where the offense is an abject failure? Doesn’t seem likely to me.

4) How much influence does Howie Roseman have beyond traditional GM responsibility of roster construction and cap/contract management? Does he help decide which coordinators to hire, which players to feature, dissect what went wrong or right on gameday, etc?

The Eagles are a GM-centric organization. Roseman’s fingerprints are all over this franchise. He definitely has a voice in decisions that are more traditionally left to the head coach. There’s no arguing that this setup hasn’t worked well for the Eagles; they’ve won two Super Bowls and been to three with Roseman as a driving factor. But the configuration does have some drawbacks, as seen in the aftermath of their championship successes.

[Editor’s note: this question was somewhat inspired by reading this article on what transpired at the end of the Doug Pederson era.]

5) What is your realistic best-case scenario for the Eagles rest of season and offseason?

The best-case scenario is that the Eagles win out!

Oh … you said “realistic.”

It behooves the Eagles to lose as many games as possible. They shouldn’t (nor won’t) “tank” in terms of players/coaches not trying to win because that’s just not how their incentives work.

But the team’s focus should be beyond the 2026 season. They need to sell some players ahead of the trade deadline. They need to part ways with some dead-end veterans and find playing time for young guys.

2026 doesn’t have to be a harbinger of more bad seasons to follow. In fact, I’m confident in saying that it won’t be. Roseman has earned the benefit of the doubt when it comes to turning things around after a bad year. I’m not saying that the Eagles will definitely win the Super Bowl in 2027. But I do feel good about their chances to be a contender again sooner than later.

There’s a lot of work to be done and the road might not be easy. But the Eagles will be back.

item.title: NFL predictions: 3 underdogs set to surprise for Bills vs. Ravens
item.description: Three Buffalo Bills underdogs who could play huge roles against Baltimore Ravens in Week 8
item.content:encoded:
The Buffalo Bills are back in action this weekend, ready for a fresh start after a relatively early bye week away from football. Since 2018, the Bills and quarterback Josh Allen are 8-0 in games after the bye. It’s a record that’s also neatly tied to former head coach Sean McDermott.

Now, new head coach Joe Brady gets his first crack at establishing his own post-bye legacy in tandem with Allen. Standing in the way are the Baltimore Ravens, a team that should be plenty motivated to reset the narrative after a crushing loss to the Cincinnati Bengals.

If the Ravens struggled to stop quarterback Joe Burrow and company last weekend, what’s in store for them against the league’s top-scoring offense on Sunday? A track meet, of sorts, may be necessary in Week 8 — with Buffalo and Baltimore potentially lighting up the scoreboard on offense.

Given the recent history between these two teams, there’s very little to plant one’s flag in the ground while staking a bold claim. What’s bold in most arenas trends typical when quarterback Lamar Jackson and Allen renew their friendship.

No one would be shocked to see Allen and/or Jackson put up five touchdowns, or even surprised to learn that running backs James Cook III and Derrick Henry took more than one football more than 50 yards to paydirt en route to a 150-plus effort on the ground.

Instead, what would reverberate across the NFL is if Bills-Ravens ended with a 9-6 score, or that Buffalo’s defense clamped down and provided the only score en route to victory. Or perhaps that Baltimore found a way to win a shootout without touchdowns from either Jackson or Henry.

It’s going to take incredible performances by unsung heroes for anyone to be surprised by Sunday’s outcome. Here are a few potentially bold options to consider…

TE Jackson Hawes scores his first TD of 2026 NFL season

For those who celebrate, National Tight Ends Day was October 25, 2026. Unfortunately, the Bills weren’t able to take part in the festivities thanks to their bye. A week later, Buffalo’s quadruple alliance at tight end returns to the field ready to party. Well, for the most part: We don’t know if Dalton Kincaid will play due to his questionable status based off a current chest injury, but it’s not a great sign to see him limited in each practice session this week following a week off.

The Bills love to run 13 personnel, and that offers plenty of chances for tight ends Dawson Knox and Jackson Hawes to see action. If Kincaid can’t go, it’s easy to land on Knox as the biggest beneficiary in terms of snaps and targets. Instead, I believe it’s Hawes who leaps into a featured role, thanks to his otherworldly blocking ability and a set of very capable hands.

Interestingly, Hawes has been a few steps below an afterthought as a receiver this season. Hawes has zero offensive stats on one target through the first six games. This comes after a rookie season in 2025 that saw Hawes make 16 catches (19 targets) for 187 yards and three touchdowns. It’s fair to say that Brady and Allen have a one-track mind regarding Hawes this season, which is status as a blocker.

That may change in Week 8. But understand this is a pretty deep dig into “bold” territory. The oddsmakers at Fanduel Sportsbook list only eight options for Jackson Hawes in Week 8, and most of them carry long, yet potentially rewarding odds.

The next touchdown pass that Josh Allen throws will vault him above Pro Football Hall of Fame quarterback Jim Kelly and to the top of the Bills’ record books as the new all-time leader in touchdown passes. Is Hawes on the receiving end of that historic moment?

Well, let’s just say there’s a possibility, albeit slight. Current options find Hawes with +5000 odds to be the game’s first touchdown scorer. There are of course a few more semi-realistic options that find Hawes as an anytime touchdown scorer (+850), anytime first-half touchdown scorer (+1600), or anytime second-half touchdown scorer (+1300).

Better yet, well if you’re looking for a really crazy option that involves Hawes. How’s +25000 odds for Hawes to be first touchdown scorer among all 1 p.m. EST games?

In all honesty, Kincaid is viewed as the tight end more likely to accomplish any one of those feats mentioned above. His questionable status does however do just enough to open the door a bit wider for a player Buffalo should do more to get involved. So you’re wondering how Hawes did against Baltimore last season, his first regular-season game? Hawes caught his lone target for 29 yards on 16 offensive snaps (hat tip to Pro Football Reference). He has plenty more to offer than that for Round 2!

RB Ty Johnson leads Bills in receiving yards

What brand of sorcery is this?! Allen’s favorite third-down specialist, Ty Johnson has roared to life since his return from a hamstring injury at the end of training camp this past August. Though perhaps still viewed as an unfortunate and unfair slight to Cook, it’s now clear that Johnson takes priority on most third downs simply because of his talent as a receiver.

Johnson is a legit threat to take any screen pass or otherwise the distance. He’s a deceptive speed demon who wastes no time getting from A to B, and then, C, D, and often Z. Still, predicting Johnson to lead the Bills in receiving yards is about as bold as it comes in Week 8.

Yes, Kincaid is questionable, as is wide receiver DJ Moore. Johnson would still have to compete with wide receivers Khalil Shakir and Keon Coleman, and on a smaller share of snaps. Johnson is similar to Shakir in ways, a pinball wizard with a more direct sort of attack. Give Johnson a football, and he’s off to the races, running around, through, and past anyone unfamiliar with his game.

What might it look like if Johnson were to lead the Bills in receiving against the Ravens? He’ll probably need north of 60 yards, which carries +1280 odds at Fanduel. Think he can do it? The last time Johnson faced the Ravens, he was held without a catch on two targets. In four games this season, Johnson has gone over 50 yards twice.

S Damar Hamlin’s play rallies D

Damar Hamlin will start at safety alongside Cole Bishop on Sunday, stepping in for safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson (suspended Week 8). Despite the concerns fans have with Gardner-Johnson’s play, and the performance of the defensive backs in total, many worry what starting Hamlin means for a 31st-ranked defensive unit.

It’s worth wondering how many of Hamlin’s plays the constant naysayers have watched over the years. Hamlin is a sound tackler who has often served as the last line of defense in scoring moments. He’s not an elite athlete by most standards, but he is an intelligent player who’s more than capable and wholly comfortable calling coverages and offensive looks from the back seven. He’s also a fantastic special teams player.

To this point, Hamlin’s football story has been dominated by an against-all-odds full recovery following a play few will ever forget, but one that he fails to remember following his body’s response to trauma. But there’s far more to Hamlin’s game than most people understand. In McDermott’s scheme, Hamlin was put in position to succeed, and did well as someone with a knack for interceptions.

I see good things happening for Hamlin against the Ravens on Sunday. Watch for him to pick off one of Jackson’s passes in a huge moment, or perhaps force a fumble of Henry or someone else. Strong play by Hamlin could be a huge part of the defense’s ability to rally toward victory in Week 8.

You might recall the last time that Hamlin started against the Ravens, a game in which he made a touchdown-saving solo tackle on Henry, and forced a fumble of Jackson.

item.title: Winless Chargers eager to play spoiler vs. Rams with healthier roster
item.description: Injuries have played a key role in the Chargers' 0-6 start to the season, but Joe Alt, Ladd McConkey and Tre' Harris are all set to play against the Rams.
item.content:encoded:
Although All-Pro safety Derwin James Jr. will miss his fourth consecutive game because of a hamstring injury, the winless Chargers are coming off their bye week with some much-needed reinforcements.

Wide receivers Ladd McConkey (concussion) and Tre’ Harris (hamstring) and offensive tackle Joe Alt (neck) are all set to play Sunday against the Rams at SoFi Stadium.

“It’s a good thing,” Chargers coach Jim Harbaugh said. “It’s good to have them back out there. Good work put in. Feel good about the preparation and feel like we’re in a good place, ready to go.”

Harris and McConkey have been the Chargers’ top two receivers when available this season. Harris leads the team in receptions (15), receiving yards (225) and targets (26), while McConkey is right behind him with 13 receptions for 200 yards on 18 targets.

Read more:Chargers vs. Rams: How to watch, start time, prediction and odds

And Alt’s return instantly improves the Chargers’ banged-up offensive line, which has allowed Justin Herbert — who carries a league-worst 29.4 quarterback rating — to be sacked nine times in the two games the offensive tackle has missed.

“Regrouping. Retooling. Thought it was a really good week of preparation,” Harbaugh said.

Offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel and his unit desperately need all hands on deck.

The Chargers are averaging a league-worst 15 points per game and are tied for the second-fewest yards per play (4.6).

“I spend all of my time focusing on the best plan for the players that we have available this week, to attack the defense we have,” McDaniel said. “And then you have to illustrate, in a good manner, what the vision is for how we’re going to play and improve the results.”

McConkey, Harris and Alt returning will help McDaniel’s cause, especially as wideout Brenen Thompson (quad/hamstring) remains out alongside key offensive linemen Rashawn Slater (ankle) and Kayode Awosika (fibula).

Read more:Staggering 74.5% of NFL players who died from 2008 to 2023 likely had CTE, study finds

Meanwhile, the Chargers’ defense, which allows the eighth-fewest passing yards per game (206.2), must hold the fort again without James, who suffered a rehab setback.

“You can’t replace Derwin,” defensive coordinator Chris O’Leary said. “It’s not possible. He’s one of the best in the league, if not the best in the league.”

That task will be even harder if cornerbacks Donte Jackson and Rodney Shelley, who are both questionable with hamstring injuries, can’t play.

“For us, our message from the offseason to now is: team defense,” O’Leary said. “Play together. We’re not going to put too much on one guy’s plate. ... And that’s really just spiked, now that Derwin’s out.

“It’s just a group effort, and I think the guys have done a great job.”

O’Leary’s defense has bent but rarely broken all season.

McDaniel’s offense, however, could use a breakout performance. And with more of Herbert’s primary targets fully healthy, there’s no better time than Sunday.

“It was much-needed,” Herbert said of the bye.

item.title: Kyren Williams, Blake Corum balance the Rams' offense. Can Sean McVay unlock their potential?
item.description: Kyren Williams and Blake Corum proved against the Raiders they can be a potent 1-2 punch for the Rams if the team can continue to maximize their skills.
item.content:encoded:
The Rams finally found it.

For one game at least, running backs Kyren Williams and Blake Corum each carried the ball nearly the same number of times, rushed for nearly the same amount of yards and each scored a touchdown last week in the Rams’ victory over the Las Vegas Raiders.

“We have similarities running the ball but also differences too,” Williams said. “And I think that’s what makes that 1-2 punch everybody keeps talking about.”

Before the victory over the Raiders, most of the conversation about the rushing attack centered around a question: When would coach and play-caller Sean McVay find a way to effectively use both?

Read more:Rams players open up about the 'double-edged sword' of CTE and football

Now the question is whether McVay and the backs can repeat or produce a similar performance Sunday against the Chargers and beyond.

McVay noted that Williams and Corum are interchangeable.

“As a play-caller, the best thing is you just call the plays,” McVay said. “It’s not like I have a specific menu of plays for Blake or for Kyren or vice versa.”

Williams, 26, is 5 feet, 9 inches, and 207 pounds. Corum, 25, is 5-8 and 202 pounds.

Williams wears jersey No. 23, Corum No. 24.

The Rams drafted Williams in the fifth round out of Notre Dame in 2022, and selected Corum in the third round out of Michigan in 2024.

“There’s a difference in their run style,” McVay said. “You’re defending different things. They’re nice complements.”

That was in full effect against the Raiders.

Williams rushed for 99 yards and a touchdown in 16 carries. Corum rushed for 93 yards and a touchdown in 17 carries.

Their effort helped the Rams take a 35-21 victory that ended a two-game losing streak and kept alive hope for a team that started the season as the Super Bowl favorite.

The two backs share a “growth mindset,” Williams said.

“It’s a great vibe, where we’re able to play off each other, not just on the football field but also in life,” he said.

They also enjoy “a healthy, competitive relationship,” Corum said.

“It’s like I want to see the best for you and he wants to see the best for me,” Corum said. “If he does something great, it’s ‘All right, can I do something greater to help the team.’

“And if I do something great, he’s like, ‘Can I do something greater.’ It’s all love, and all for the team.”

Williams, a 2023 Pro Bowl player, signed a three-year extension before last season that included $23 million in guarantees. He went into this season having rushed for at least 1,144 yards in each of the last three seasons, including more than 1,200 in each of the last two.

The game against the Raiders is what the Rams envisioned — but did not achieve — last season when they aimed to reduce Williams’ workload as a way of keeping him fresh for the latter part of the season and the playoffs.

In 2025, Williams rushed for 1,252 yards and 10 touchdowns in 259 carries. Corum gained 746 yards and scored six touchdowns in 145 carries.

So far this season, Williams has rushed for 492 yards and five touchdowns in 96 carries. He also has 32 receptions for 239 yards and a touchdown.

Corum has rushed for 316 yards and two touchdowns in 64 carries. He has 10 catches for 99 yards and a touchdown.

Read more:NFL Week 8 picks: Lions beat 6-0 Vikings; Steelers prevail over Browns

“I haven’t been a part of that before where you haven’t thought to yourself, ‘OK, we want to lean on these types of plays when this guy’s in and these types of plays when the other guy’s in,’” quarterback Matthew Stafford said. “I think you’re really comfortable with both those guys doing everything we ask of a halfback in this offense.”

Offensive linemen said they often are unaware which running back is in the game — until they look up to see who is celebrating in the end zone.

“It’s crazy to say — but legit,” guard Kevin Dotson said. “It feels just like a plug and play. I don’t know who’s really in, and it doesn’t really matter.

“I know they can make it happen.”
